questions.question: What is the difference between dcb0160 and DCB0129?
questions.answer: DCB0129 applies to the manufacturer of a health IT system; DCB0160 applies to the health or care organisation that deploys and uses it. DCB0129 covers clinical risk management during the development and maintenance of the system; DCB0160 covers it during deployment, use, maintenance and decommissioning. Both are mandatory NHS England information standards under section 250 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, and each requires a named Clinical Safety Officer.
questions.shortAnswer: The two standards split clinical safety along the supply chain. **DCB0129** sets clinical-risk-management requirements for the **manufacturer** of a health IT system — its development and maintenance. **DCB0160** sets the equivalent requirements for the **health or care organisation that deploys and uses** that system. Both are mandatory NHS England information standards published under **section 250 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012**, and each requires a named **Clinical Safety Officer**.

questions.question: What is the difference between a controller and a processor under the GDPR?
questions.answer: The controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data — it decides why and how data is processed. The processor processes personal data on behalf of the controller — it acts under the controller's instructions. The distinction determines which GDPR obligations apply to each party.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 4(7) defines the controller as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Article 4(8) defines the processor as the entity that processes personal data on behalf of the controller. The controller makes the key decisions: what data to collect, why to collect it, how long to keep it, and who to share it with. The processor carries out processing operations under the controller's instructions — such as a cloud provider hosting data, a payroll company processing salaries, or an email service provider sending marketing communications. Both have GDPR obligations, but the controller bears primary responsibility for compliance.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 4(7) — Definition of controller
GDPR Article 4(8) — Definition of processor
GDPR Article 26 — Joint controllers
GDPR Article 28 — Processor obligations and DPA requirements
GDPR Article 30 — Records of processing activities

questions.question: Does the DMA apply to cloud service providers?
questions.answer: Cloud computing services are listed as one of the ten categories of core platform services in the DMA (Article 2(2)(f)). A cloud provider could be designated as a gatekeeper if it meets the three criteria: significant market impact, important gateway status, and entrenched position. As of 2025, no cloud provider has been separately designated as a gatekeeper, though Amazon and Microsoft — both designated as gatekeepers for other services — also operate major cloud platforms. The Commission continues to assess whether standalone cloud gatekeeper designations are warranted.
questions.shortAnswer: Cloud computing is a DMA core platform service, but no cloud provider has been designated as a gatekeeper specifically for cloud services yet. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are operated by companies already designated as gatekeepers for other services (marketplace, operating system, search), but the cloud-specific obligations only apply if the cloud service itself is separately designated. The Commission is actively monitoring cloud market concentration.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 2(2)(f) — Cloud computing services as a core platform service
DMA Article 3 — Gatekeeper designation criteria applicable to cloud providers
DMA Article 5(2) — Data combination restrictions
DMA Article 6(9) — Data portability obligations
EU Data Act Articles 23-31 — Cloud switching and interoperability (separate regulation)

questions.question: Does the DMA apply to non-EU companies?
questions.answer: Yes. The DMA applies to any undertaking that provides a core platform service to business users and end users in the EU, regardless of where the company is headquartered. All currently designated gatekeepers are US or Chinese companies: Alphabet (US), Amazon (US), Apple (US), ByteDance (China), Meta (US), and Microsoft (US). The DMA's jurisdictional reach is based on where the service is provided and used, not where the company is incorporated or headquartered.
questions.shortAnswer: The DMA is explicitly designed to regulate the largest global digital platforms, which are predominantly US-based. It applies wherever a core platform service is offered to EU users and business users, regardless of the company's headquarters. Non-compliance by non-EU companies carries the same penalties — up to 10% of worldwide turnover — and the Commission has enforcement mechanisms including requiring compliance measures before allowing continued operation in the EU.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 1(2) — Territorial scope (services provided to EU users)

DMA Article 18 — Behavioural and structural remedies

questions.question: What are the DMA's data portability requirements?
questions.answer: The DMA requires gatekeepers to provide effective data portability under Article 6(9), going beyond the GDPR's portability right. Gatekeepers must provide end users and authorised third parties with effective, high-quality, continuous and real-time access to data generated by the end user's activity on the gatekeeper's platform, including through tools that facilitate the exercise of data portability. This means not just one-time data export, but continuous access APIs that allow users to move their data and activity history to competing services.
questions.shortAnswer: DMA data portability goes significantly beyond GDPR Article 20. Gatekeepers must provide not just one-time data downloads, but continuous, real-time access to user-generated data through APIs and tools. This enables users to simultaneously use a gatekeeper's service and a competing service, with their data flowing to both in real time — breaking the data lock-in that sustains gatekeeper market power.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 6(9) — End-user data portability (continuous, real-time access)

questions.question: What are the DMA's interoperability requirements?
questions.answer: The DMA requires gatekeepers to provide interoperability for number-independent interpersonal communication services (messaging apps) under Article 7. Gatekeepers must enable end users of third-party messaging services to exchange text messages, images, voice messages, videos, voice calls, and video calls with users of the gatekeeper's service. Implementation is phased: basic text and image interoperability within two years of designation, group messaging and group calls within four years. End-to-end encryption must be maintained where technically feasible.
questions.shortAnswer: Gatekeeper messaging apps (WhatsApp, Messenger, iMessage) must allow users on other messaging platforms to send and receive messages, images, voice messages, and eventually make calls with gatekeeper users. This is being rolled out in phases over four years. End-to-end encryption must be preserved. The goal is to break the network effects that lock users into dominant messaging platforms.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 7(1) — Basic interoperability obligation for messaging services
DMA Article 7(2) — Phased implementation timeline (2 years for basic, 4 years for group and calls)

questions.question: What are the DMA obligations for app stores?
questions.answer: App stores designated as gatekeeper core platform services must allow developers to use third-party payment systems (Article 5(7)), permit sideloading of apps from alternative sources (Article 6(4)), refrain from requiring developers to use the gatekeeper's identity or payment services (Article 5(7)-(8)), allow app developers to communicate with end users about offers outside the app store (Article 5(4)), and provide fair, non-discriminatory ranking of third-party apps alongside the gatekeeper's own apps (Article 6(5)).
questions.shortAnswer: App store gatekeepers (Apple's App Store, Google Play) must allow alternative payment systems, permit sideloading, stop forcing developers to use gatekeeper services, let developers communicate directly with users about alternative offers, and rank third-party apps fairly. These obligations fundamentally reshape the app store business model by breaking down the walled-garden approach that has characterised mobile platforms.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 5(4) — Right of business users to communicate offers to end users

DMA Article 5(8) — Prohibition on requiring gatekeeper identity services
DMA Article 6(4) — Sideloading and alternative app store obligations

questions.question: What are the DMA penalties for big tech non-compliance?
questions.answer: DMA penalties for non-compliance are among the highest in EU regulation. First-offence fines can reach 10% of worldwide annual turnover. Repeat offenders face fines up to 20% of worldwide turnover. Periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover can be imposed for ongoing violations. In cases of systematic non-compliance, the Commission can impose structural remedies including requiring divestiture of business units — a power unprecedented in EU digital regulation.
questions.shortAnswer: DMA fines reach 10% of global revenue for first offences and 20% for repeated violations. For a company with $300 billion in annual revenue, that translates to $30-60 billion in potential fines. The Commission can also impose daily penalty payments and, in extreme cases, force structural changes like breaking up business units. These are the largest potential penalties in EU digital regulation.
relevantArticles: DMA Article 12(1) — Fines up to 10% of worldwide turnover for non-compliance
DMA Article 12(2) — Fines up to 20% for repeat non-compliance

questions.question: What is the DMA's ban on self-preferencing?
questions.answer: The DMA prohibits gatekeepers from treating their own products and services more favourably than those of third parties in ranking, display, and access on their platforms. Under Article 6(5), gatekeepers must not favour their own offerings in search results, app store rankings, or marketplace listings. The gatekeeper must apply fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory conditions to ranking and must publish the main parameters used for ranking, along with the reasons for the relative importance of those parameters.
questions.shortAnswer: Gatekeepers cannot rank, display, or promote their own products above competing third-party products on their platforms. Google cannot prioritise Google Shopping in search results. Amazon cannot rank Amazon Basics products above equivalent third-party products in marketplace search. Apple cannot preferentially surface its own apps in the App Store. Ranking must be based on fair, transparent, and non-discriminatory criteria that are published and applied equally.

questions.question: What are the DMA's sideloading requirements?
questions.answer: Under DMA Article 6(4), gatekeepers operating an operating system must allow the installation of third-party apps and app stores outside the gatekeeper's own app store. This 'sideloading' requirement means Apple must allow iOS users to install apps from sources other than the App Store, and Google must ensure Android sideloading is not unnecessarily restricted. Gatekeepers may implement proportionate security measures (such as malware scanning) but cannot use security concerns as a pretext to block or discourage alternative app distribution.
questions.shortAnswer: Gatekeepers must allow apps to be installed from outside their official app stores. Apple's implementation of this requirement in the EU allows alternative app marketplaces on iOS, though the specifics of Apple's compliance have been contested. Google's Android already allows sideloading but must ensure the process is not unreasonably burdensome. Gatekeepers can implement security checks but cannot use them to effectively block alternative distribution.

questions.question: What is the difference between the DMA and DSA?
questions.answer: The Digital Markets Act (DMA) and Digital Services Act (DSA) are complementary EU regulations with different objectives. The DMA regulates competition by imposing obligations on large platforms designated as gatekeepers, aiming to ensure contestable and fair digital markets. The DSA regulates content by imposing due diligence obligations on online intermediaries, aiming to create a safer online environment. The DMA targets market structure and anti-competitive behaviour; the DSA targets illegal content, transparency, and user safety.
questions.shortAnswer: The DMA is about market competition — it stops big tech from abusing their gatekeeper position. The DSA is about online safety — it requires platforms to tackle illegal content, be transparent about algorithms, and protect users. Different laws, different goals, different obligations. A large platform like Meta is subject to both: the DMA for its gatekeeper behaviour, and the DSA for its content moderation responsibilities.

questions.question: Do I need a conformity assessment for my AI system?
questions.answer: You need a conformity assessment if your AI system is classified as high-risk under Article 6 of the EU AI Act. Most high-risk AI systems can use self-assessment (internal control), but biometric identification systems and critical infrastructure AI typically require third-party assessment by a notified body.
questions.shortAnswer: Conformity assessment is mandatory for all high-risk AI systems before they can be placed on the EU market or put into service. Article 43 establishes two pathways. The default is internal control (Annex VI) — essentially a structured self-assessment where the provider evaluates compliance against all Chapter III requirements and documents the results. The exception is third-party assessment by a notified body (Annex VII), which is required for remote biometric identification AI systems listed in Annex III point 1 and for high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products already requiring notified body assessment under Annex I legislation.

questions.question: Do I need a Data Protection Officer (DPO) under the GDPR?
questions.answer: You must appoint a DPO if you are a public authority, if your core activities involve regular and systematic monitoring of individuals on a large scale, or if your core activities involve large-scale processing of special category data or criminal conviction data. Many organisations appoint one voluntarily as best practice.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 37 requires the appointment of a DPO in three situations. First, the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except courts acting in their judicial capacity). Second, the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations which, by their nature, scope, or purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale. Third, the core activities consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data (Article 9) or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences (Article 10). Outside these mandatory cases, any organisation may voluntarily appoint a DPO.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 37 — Designation of the DPO

questions.question: Do I need a privacy policy under the GDPR?
questions.answer: Yes. Articles 13 and 14 require you to provide specific information to data subjects about how you process their personal data. This information is typically delivered through a privacy policy (also called a privacy notice). The policy must be concise, transparent, intelligible, easily accessible, and written in clear and plain language.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR requires transparency about personal data processing through Articles 13 and 14. While the term "privacy policy" does not appear in the GDPR, the detailed information requirements effectively mandate a comprehensive privacy notice. Article 13 applies when you collect data directly from the data subject. Article 14 applies when you obtain data from a source other than the data subject. Both require disclosure of specific information including the controller's identity, processing purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention periods, and data subject rights.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 13 — Information for direct data collection
GDPR Article 14 — Information for indirect data collection
GDPR Article 12 — Transparent information and communication
GDPR Article 83(5)(b) — Fines for transparency violations

questions.question: Do I need to register my AI system in the EU database?
questions.answer: Yes, if your AI system is high-risk. Article 49 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to register them in the EU database before placing them on the market. Deployers of high-risk systems must also register their use. The database is publicly accessible and serves transparency and market surveillance purposes.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 49 establishes a mandatory EU database for high-risk AI systems. Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market or putting it into service, the provider must register it in the database. Deployers of high-risk AI systems under Annex III must also register their use of the system. The database is managed by the European Commission and is publicly accessible, creating a transparency mechanism that allows anyone to see which high-risk AI systems are operating in the EU and who is responsible for them.
relevantArticles: EU AI Act Article 49 — Registration in the EU database
EU AI Act Article 71 — EU database establishment and management
EU AI Act Article 47 — EU declaration of conformity
EU AI Act Article 48 — CE marking

questions.question: Does the CCPA apply to my business?
questions.answer: The CCPA applies to for-profit businesses that collect California residents' personal information and meet at least one of three thresholds: annual gross revenue exceeding $25 million, buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more California consumers or households per year, or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information. The law applies regardless of where the business is physically located.
questions.shortAnswer: The CCPA applies if your for-profit business collects personal information from California residents and meets any one of three thresholds: $25 million in annual gross revenue, processing data of 100,000 or more consumers or households annually, or deriving 50% or more of revenue from selling or sharing personal information. Non-profits and government agencies are generally exempt.

questions.question: Does the Cyber Resilience Act apply to software?
questions.answer: Yes. The CRA applies to products with digital elements, which includes both hardware and software — standalone software, firmware, operating systems, applications, and software components. Any software placed on the EU market that can connect to a device or network is in scope, unless specifically excluded (e.g., medical devices, vehicles, or aviation software already regulated under other EU legislation).
questions.shortAnswer: The CRA (Regulation 2024/2847) applies to "products with digital elements" — defined as any software or hardware product and its remote data processing solutions, including software or hardware components placed on the market separately. Software is explicitly in scope. This includes standalone desktop and mobile applications, operating systems and firmware, software libraries and SDKs distributed commercially, cloud-connected software components, and IoT device firmware. The CRA excludes products already regulated under sector-specific EU legislation that achieves equivalent cybersecurity outcomes (medical devices under MDR, vehicles under vehicle type-approval, aviation under EASA regulations).

questions.question: Does DORA apply to my company?
questions.answer: DORA applies to virtually all EU-regulated financial entities including banks, investment firms, insurance companies, payment institutions, crypto-asset service providers, and more. It also applies to critical ICT third-party service providers designated by the European Supervisory Authorities. DORA has been applicable since 17 January 2025.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA (Regulation 2022/2554) applies to 21 categories of financial entity listed in Article 2(1), including credit institutions, payment institutions, account information service providers, electronic money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers, central securities depositories, central counterparties, trading venues, trade repositories, alternative investment fund managers, management companies, insurance and reinsurance undertakings, insurance intermediaries, institutions for occupational retirement provision, credit rating agencies, crowdfunding service providers, and securitisation repositories. It also applies to ICT third-party service providers designated as critical by the European Supervisory Authorities under Article 31.

questions.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to US companies?
questions.answer: Yes. The EU AI Act applies to any company — regardless of where it is based — that places AI systems on the EU market or whose AI system outputs are used within the EU. US companies selling to EU customers, or whose AI-generated outputs affect EU residents, are within scope.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act has extraterritorial reach. Under Article 2, it applies to providers who place AI systems on the EU market regardless of whether they are established in the EU or a third country, deployers of AI systems who are located within the EU, and providers and deployers located outside the EU where the output produced by the AI system is used in the EU. If your US company sells AI products to EU customers, provides AI-powered services accessible in the EU, or builds AI systems whose outputs are relied upon by EU-based organisations, the Act applies to you.

questions.question: Does my organisation need to complete the DSPT?
questions.answer: If your organisation accesses NHS patient data or connects to NHS systems, you generally must complete the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) each year. This covers NHS trusts, GP practices, pharmacies, dentists, social-care providers, and IT suppliers or processors handling NHS data. The cycle runs to the financial year and the submission deadline falls on 30 June; the last cycle we have confirmed against the toolkit was 2025/26 (version 8), which closed on 30 June 2026. Check dsptoolkit.nhs.uk for the dates of the cycle you are in.
questions.shortAnswer: If your organisation has access to NHS patient data or connects to NHS systems, you almost certainly need to complete the Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT), and you need to do it every year. This includes NHS trusts and foundation trusts, GP practices, pharmacies, dentists, opticians, social-care providers, and the IT suppliers and data processors that handle NHS data on their behalf. The submission deadline falls on 30 June each year; the 2025/26 return closed on 30 June 2026.

questions.question: Does NIS2 apply to my company?
questions.answer: NIS2 applies if your company operates in one of 18 covered sectors and meets the size threshold (medium or large enterprise — 50+ employees or 10M+ EUR turnover). Some entities are in scope regardless of size, including DNS providers, TLD registries, qualified trust service providers, and sole providers of essential services in a member state.
questions.shortAnswer: NIS2 (Directive 2022/2555) applies based on two criteria: sector and size. Your company is in scope if it operates in one of 11 "highly critical" sectors (Annex I) or 7 "other critical" sectors (Annex II), AND it qualifies as a medium or large enterprise under the EU SME definition (50+ employees or annual turnover/balance sheet exceeding 10 million euros). Certain entities are in scope regardless of size: providers of public electronic communications networks, trust service providers, TLD name registries, DNS service providers, and sole providers of a service in a member state that is essential for the maintenance of critical societal or economic activities. Member states had until 17 October 2024 to transpose NIS2 into national law.

questions.question: Does DORA apply to fintech companies?
questions.answer: It depends on whether the fintech holds an EU financial services licence. Payment institutions, electronic money institutions, crypto-asset service providers, and other licensed fintechs are explicitly in DORA scope. Unlicensed fintechs are not directly subject to DORA but may be caught as ICT third-party providers to regulated financial entities.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA applies to fintechs based on their regulatory status, not their business model. If a fintech holds an EU financial services authorisation — payment institution, electronic money institution, investment firm, crypto-asset service provider, crowdfunding service provider — it is within DORA scope and must comply with all applicable chapters. If a fintech operates without a financial services licence (providing technology to licensed entities, operating under regulatory exemptions, or serving non-financial markets), it is not directly subject to DORA but may face indirect obligations as an ICT third-party service provider.

questions.question: Does DORA apply to insurance companies?
questions.answer: Yes. DORA Article 2(1) explicitly includes insurance undertakings, reinsurance undertakings, insurance intermediaries, and institutions for occupational retirement provision. Insurance companies must comply with the full DORA framework including ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party risk management.
questions.shortAnswer: Insurance and reinsurance undertakings are explicitly within DORA scope under Article 2(1)(j) and (k). Insurance intermediaries meeting the conditions of Directive 2016/97 are also in scope under Article 2(1)(l). Institutions for occupational retirement provision (IORPs) are covered under Article 2(1)(m). All must comply with DORA's ICT risk management framework (Chapter II), incident reporting obligations (Chapter III), digital operational resilience testing (Chapter IV), and ICT third-party risk management (Chapter V). EIOPA is the relevant European Supervisory Authority for insurance sector DORA oversight.
relevantArticles: DORA Article 2(1)(j)-(m) — Insurance entities in scope

questions.question: What is a critical ICT third-party provider under DORA?
questions.answer: A critical ICT third-party service provider (CTPP) is an ICT provider designated by the ESAs as systemically important to the financial sector. Designation criteria include the number and importance of financial entities relying on the provider, the provider's substitutability, and its significance to the sector. CTPPs face direct ESA oversight through a Lead Overseer.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA Articles 31-44 establish a novel oversight framework for critical ICT third-party service providers. The three ESAs (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA) jointly designate providers as critical based on the systemic impact that a large-scale operational failure of the provider would have on the financial entities it serves, the systemic character or importance of the financial entities relying on it, the degree of substitutability of the provider, and the number of member states where the provider operates. Designated CTPPs are assigned a Lead Overseer (one of the ESAs) who can conduct inspections, issue recommendations, and impose penalty payments.

questions.question: What are DORA's ICT risk requirements?
questions.answer: DORA Chapter II (Articles 5-16) requires financial entities to establish a comprehensive ICT risk management framework covering governance, risk identification, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, learning and evolving, and communication. The framework must be documented, regularly tested, and approved by the management body.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA Chapter II establishes detailed ICT risk management requirements. Article 5 requires the management body to define, approve, oversee, and be accountable for the ICT risk management framework. Article 6 requires a comprehensive framework covering identification, protection, detection, response, recovery, and lessons learned. Articles 7-13 detail specific requirements for ICT systems and tools, identification of ICT risks, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, backup and restoration, and learning and evolving. Article 14 covers communication during ICT-related incidents. Article 16 provides a simplified framework for microenterprises.

questions.question: What is the DORA incident reporting timeline?
questions.answer: DORA requires a three-stage incident reporting process: an initial notification within 4 hours of classifying a major ICT-related incident, an intermediate report within 72 hours with updated information, and a final report within one month including root cause analysis and recovery details.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 19 requires financial entities to report major ICT-related incidents to the competent authority using a three-stage process. Initial notification: within 4 hours of the incident being classified as major, and no later than 24 hours after the entity becomes aware of the incident. Intermediate report: within 72 hours of the initial notification, providing updated information and an initial assessment. Final report: within one month of the intermediate report, including root cause analysis, description of recovery actions, and quantification of impact. This timeline is more compressed than NIS2's equivalent, reflecting the systemic importance of financial services.
relevantArticles: DORA Article 19 — Reporting of major ICT-related incidents

questions.question: What are DORA's penetration testing requirements?
questions.answer: DORA Chapter IV requires all financial entities to conduct digital operational resilience testing, and specific entities must undergo advanced threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years. TLPT tests must follow recognised frameworks (TIBER-EU), be conducted by qualified external testers, and cover critical functions.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA Chapter IV (Articles 24-27) establishes a two-tier testing framework. The first tier applies to all financial entities: they must conduct a range of digital operational resilience tests including vulnerability assessments and scans, open source analyses, network security assessments, gap analyses, physical security reviews, compatibility testing, scenario-based testing, and penetration testing. The second tier applies to entities identified by competent authorities: they must conduct advanced threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years, following the TIBER-EU framework or equivalent recognised methodology. TLPT must be conducted by external testers with appropriate qualifications.

questions.question: What are DORA's third-party ICT risk rules?
questions.answer: DORA Chapter V establishes comprehensive requirements for managing risks from ICT third-party service providers used by financial entities. Key requirements include: maintaining a complete register of all ICT third-party arrangements, conducting pre-contractual risk assessments, including mandatory contractual provisions (access rights, audit rights, incident notification, exit strategies), monitoring provider performance and security, and managing concentration risk. The European Supervisory Authorities can designate critical ICT third-party service providers for direct EU-level oversight, creating a new regulatory layer for major cloud and technology providers serving the financial sector.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA transforms how financial entities manage their technology suppliers. Every ICT arrangement must be documented in a register. Every contract must include specific provisions covering security, audit, incident notification, and exit. Critical ICT providers (think major cloud platforms) face direct oversight from EU supervisory authorities. Financial entities must assess whether they are over-concentrated on single providers and develop exit strategies for all critical arrangements. This is the most prescriptive third-party risk management framework in any sector globally.

questions.question: What are DORA's third-party ICT risk requirements?
questions.answer: DORA Chapter V requires financial entities to manage ICT third-party risk through a comprehensive framework. This includes maintaining a register of all ICT third-party arrangements, conducting due diligence before entering contracts, including specific contractual provisions, and assessing concentration risk. Critical ICT providers face direct ESA oversight.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA Chapter V (Articles 28-44) establishes detailed requirements for managing ICT third-party risk. Financial entities must adopt and regularly review a strategy on ICT third-party risk, maintain a complete register of all ICT third-party contractual arrangements (Article 28(3)), conduct adequate due diligence before entering ICT third-party arrangements, include specific mandatory contractual provisions (Article 30), and assess ICT concentration risk at entity and sector level. Articles 31-44 establish the oversight framework for critical ICT third-party service providers, where designated providers face direct supervision by a Lead Overseer.

questions.question: What is the difference between DORA and NIS2?
questions.answer: DORA is a sector-specific regulation for the financial sector focused on digital operational resilience. NIS2 is a horizontal cybersecurity directive covering 18 sectors. DORA takes precedence (lex specialis) for financial entities on ICT risk management and incident reporting. Financial entities primarily comply with DORA, though NIS2 may apply for non-ICT security aspects.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA and NIS2 both address cybersecurity resilience but operate at different levels. NIS2 is horizontal — it sets baseline cybersecurity requirements across 18 sectors. DORA is vertical — it establishes detailed digital operational resilience requirements specifically for the financial sector. Under the lex specialis principle (NIS2 Article 4), DORA takes precedence where it applies. Financial entities comply with DORA for ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party risk management, rather than the equivalent NIS2 provisions.

questions.question: When is a DPIA required for AI systems?
questions.answer: A Data Protection Impact Assessment is required under GDPR Article 35 whenever AI-based processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This includes AI systems that perform systematic and extensive profiling with significant effects, process special category data at scale, or systematically monitor publicly accessible areas. The EU AI Act adds a complementary fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems, and the EDPB has confirmed that most AI systems processing personal data will trigger the DPIA threshold.
questions.shortAnswer: A DPIA is required whenever an AI system's processing of personal data is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. In practice, most AI systems that process personal data will meet this threshold because they typically involve at least two of the criteria the EDPB has identified as DPIA triggers: evaluation or scoring, automated decision-making with legal or significant effects, systematic monitoring, processing of sensitive data, and innovative use of new technologies.

questions.question: What does the DSA require for algorithmic transparency?
questions.answer: The DSA requires online platforms to disclose in their terms of service the main parameters used in recommender systems and any options for users to modify those parameters (Article 27). VLOPs must additionally offer at least one recommender system option not based on profiling (Article 38), include recommender system parameters in systemic risk assessments (Article 34), provide recommender system data to researchers (Article 40), and subject their algorithmic systems to independent audit (Article 37).
questions.shortAnswer: All platforms must disclose the main parameters driving their recommender systems and give users options to influence recommendations. VLOPs must go further: they must offer a recommendation option that does not rely on user profiling, assess whether their algorithms create systemic risks, make algorithmic data available to researchers, and undergo independent audits of their algorithmic practices.

questions.question: Does the DSA apply to online marketplaces?
questions.answer: Yes. Online marketplaces are online platforms under the DSA and face all platform obligations plus additional marketplace-specific requirements. Under Article 30, marketplaces must collect and verify trader identity information (know-your-business-customer), make trader information available to consumers, and design their interfaces to enable traders to comply with product safety and consumer protection obligations. Marketplaces must also comply with notice-and-action, transparency reporting, and content moderation requirements for product listings.
questions.shortAnswer: Online marketplaces face the full suite of DSA platform obligations plus additional duties specific to facilitating commercial transactions. They must verify seller identities, provide seller information to buyers, and design their platforms to help sellers comply with product safety rules. If the marketplace reaches VLOP size (45 million EU users), additional obligations for systemic risk assessment and independent audit apply.

questions.question: Does the DSA apply to search engines?
questions.answer: Yes. The DSA applies to online search engines as a category of intermediary service. Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs) — those with 45 million or more monthly active EU users — face the same enhanced obligations as VLOPs, including systemic risk assessments, independent audits, and researcher data access. Google Search has been designated as a VLOSE. Smaller search engines face basic intermediary obligations but not the enhanced VLOP/VLOSE requirements.
questions.shortAnswer: Search engines are covered by the DSA. Large search engines (45M+ EU users) are designated as VLOSEs and face the most intensive obligations — identical to those for VLOPs. Google Search is the primary designated VLOSE. Smaller search engines face basic intermediary obligations including transparency reporting and terms of service requirements but not the enhanced systemic risk and audit obligations.

questions.question: What are the DSA's content moderation requirements?
questions.answer: The DSA requires all online platforms to establish notice-and-action mechanisms for illegal content (Article 16), provide clear terms of service explaining content moderation policies (Article 14), give reasons for content moderation decisions (Article 17), and offer internal complaint-handling systems for users affected by moderation decisions (Article 20). Platforms must not make content moderation decisions based solely on automated means without human review for decisions that significantly affect users. VLOPs face additional obligations including systemic risk assessments of content moderation practices.
questions.shortAnswer: Every online platform must have clear content rules, a system for users to report illegal content, an obligation to act on valid reports, a requirement to explain moderation decisions to affected users, and an internal appeal process. Purely automated content moderation decisions must include meaningful human review options. VLOPs must additionally assess whether their moderation practices create systemic risks.

questions.question: How does the DSA handle illegal content reporting?
questions.answer: The DSA establishes a structured notice-and-action framework under Article 16 requiring all hosting services to provide easily accessible, user-friendly mechanisms for reporting illegal content. Notices must allow identification of the specific content, explain why it is illegal, and include the notifier's contact information. Platforms must process notices in a timely, diligent, and objective manner, communicate their decision to the notifier, and inform the content provider. Trusted flaggers receive priority processing of their notices.
questions.shortAnswer: Anyone can report illegal content to a platform through a standardised notice mechanism. Platforms must make reporting easy, process reports promptly, and explain their decisions to both the reporter and the content creator. Trusted flaggers — entities certified by national authorities for their expertise — get priority handling. Repeated submission of manifestly unfounded notices can lead to suspension of the reporter's access to the notice mechanism.

questions.question: What are the DSA penalties for online platforms?
questions.answer: DSA penalties can reach up to 6% of the worldwide annual turnover of the service provider for infringements of DSA obligations. For the supply of incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information, or failure to comply with inspections, fines can reach 1% of annual worldwide turnover. Periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover can be imposed for ongoing non-compliance. National Digital Services Coordinators enforce against non-VLOP platforms, while the European Commission enforces directly against VLOPs.
questions.shortAnswer: DSA fines reach 6% of global revenue for substantive violations — lower than the DMA's 10% but still significant. For a company with EUR 100 billion revenue, that means EUR 6 billion in potential fines. Daily penalties of up to 5% of daily turnover add pressure for ongoing violations. Enforcement is split: the Commission supervises VLOPs directly; national authorities supervise smaller platforms.

questions.question: What are the DSA's transparency reporting requirements?
questions.answer: The DSA requires all online intermediaries to publish annual transparency reports covering content moderation activities. Platforms must report the number of orders received from Member State authorities (Article 15), the number of notices received and actions taken (Article 15), and the use of automated content moderation tools and their accuracy (Article 15). VLOPs face additional transparency requirements including biannual reporting on systemic risks, recommender system parameters, and data access for researchers (Articles 34, 40, 42).
questions.shortAnswer: Every online intermediary must publish at least annual transparency reports detailing their content moderation activities, orders received from authorities, and use of automated tools. VLOPs must report more frequently and more comprehensively, including systemic risk findings and recommender system details. Reports must be publicly available, machine-readable, and accessible in at least one official EU language.

questions.question: What are trusted flaggers under the DSA?
questions.answer: Trusted flaggers are entities granted special status by national Digital Services Coordinators under DSA Article 22 to submit priority content reports to online platforms. To qualify, an entity must demonstrate particular expertise and competence in detecting, identifying, and notifying illegal content, be independent from any online platform, and carry out its activities diligently, accurately, and objectively. Notices from trusted flaggers must be processed by platforms on a priority basis, though platforms retain the obligation to make their own independent assessment of legality.
questions.shortAnswer: Trusted flaggers are officially recognised experts at identifying illegal content — consumer protection organisations, anti-hate speech groups, intellectual property enforcement bodies, or child safety organisations. Their reports get fast-tracked by platforms but do not automatically result in content removal. Platforms must still make their own assessment. The system channels expertise into the content moderation process while maintaining platform decision-making responsibility.

questions.question: What is the difference between the DSA and DMA?
questions.answer: The DSA (Digital Services Act) regulates content and safety obligations for all online intermediaries, focusing on illegal content removal, transparency, and user protection. The DMA (Digital Markets Act) regulates competition by imposing specific obligations on gatekeepers — the largest digital platforms — to ensure fair and contestable markets. The DSA applies broadly (all online intermediaries, with enhanced duties for larger platforms); the DMA applies narrowly (only designated gatekeepers). They are complementary regulations addressing different aspects of the digital economy.
questions.shortAnswer: DSA = online safety and content responsibility. DMA = digital market competition. The DSA tells platforms how to handle content and protect users. The DMA tells gatekeepers how to treat business users and competitors fairly. A platform like Meta faces DSA duties for content moderation and DMA duties for market behaviour. Different regulations, different objectives, often applying to the same companies simultaneously.

questions.question: What is in the NHS DTAC checklist?
questions.answer: The NHS England Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) covers five areas a supplier must evidence: clinical safety (DCB0129/DCB0160), data protection (UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and the Data Security and Protection Toolkit), technical security, interoperability, and usability and accessibility. The first four are assessed; usability and accessibility receives a separate conformity rating.
questions.shortAnswer: The NHS England Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) is the national baseline assessment that NHS and adult social care buyers apply to a digital health product before procurement. It spans five areas: **clinical safety**, **data protection**, **technical security**, **interoperability**, and **usability and accessibility**. The first four sections are assessed against defined standards; usability and accessibility is captured as a separate conformity rating.

questions.question: What are the DTAC requirements for NHS suppliers?
questions.answer: NHS England's Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) assesses digital health products across five areas: clinical safety (DCB0129 with a Clinical Safety Officer), data protection (a published DSPT plus a DPIA), technical security (Cyber Essentials and penetration testing are commonly expected), interoperability, and usability and accessibility (the refreshed DTAC references WCAG 2.2 AA). Suppliers complete a DTAC form with supporting evidence per product version.
questions.shortAnswer: The Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC) is NHS England's baseline assessment for digital health technologies, covering five areas: clinical safety, data protection, technical security, interoperability, and usability and accessibility. Suppliers complete a DTAC form and supply supporting evidence for each product version; NHS organisations use that completed form when assessing and procuring the product. DTAC is a procurement and assurance criteria set, not a standalone certificate — there is no pass/fail "DTAC badge."

questions.question: How does eIDAS 2.0 ensure cross-border recognition of digital identity?
questions.answer: eIDAS 2.0 ensures cross-border recognition through mandatory mutual recognition of European Digital Identity Wallets and their credentials across all EU member states. When a citizen of one member state presents their wallet credentials in another member state, the receiving party must accept them with the same legal effect as domestically issued credentials. The regulation establishes a common technical architecture, interoperability framework, and trust infrastructure through EU Trusted Lists that enable seamless cross-border verification of identity and attribute credentials.
questions.shortAnswer: Cross-border recognition under eIDAS 2.0 works through three mechanisms: mandatory mutual recognition of wallet credentials, a common technical interoperability framework (the Architecture Reference Framework), and the EU Trusted Lists that publish the qualified status of trust service providers and wallet issuers. When a French citizen presents their EUDIW to a German bank, the bank can verify the credential's authenticity through the trust framework and must accept it with the same legal standing as a German identity document. This eliminates the fragmentation of digital identity across EU borders.
relevantArticles: eIDAS 2.0 Article 5a(4) — Cross-border recognition of wallet credentials

questions.question: Are electronic signatures legally valid under eIDAS 2.0?
questions.answer: Yes. eIDAS 2.0 establishes a comprehensive legal framework for electronic signatures across the EU. The regulation recognises three levels: simple electronic signatures (any electronic data attached to other data and used for signing), advanced electronic signatures (uniquely linked to the signatory with sole control), and qualified electronic signatures (created with a qualified device and based on a qualified certificate). A qualified electronic signature has the legal effect equivalent to a handwritten signature and must be recognised across all EU member states.
questions.shortAnswer: Electronic signatures are legally valid throughout the EU under eIDAS. The critical question is not whether an electronic signature is valid, but which level is required for a specific use case. Simple electronic signatures cannot be denied legal effect solely because they are electronic (Article 25), but they provide the least evidentiary weight. Advanced electronic signatures provide stronger authentication and integrity guarantees. Qualified electronic signatures provide maximum legal certainty — they are the only type that automatically has legal equivalence to handwritten signatures across all member states.

questions.question: What are qualified trust services under eIDAS 2.0?
questions.answer: Qualified trust services under eIDAS 2.0 are electronic services that meet stringent regulatory requirements and are supervised by national authorities. They include qualified electronic signatures, qualified electronic seals, qualified time stamps, qualified electronic delivery services, qualified website authentication certificates, qualified electronic attestations of attributes, qualified electronic archiving services, and qualified electronic ledgers. Qualified trust services have the highest legal standing — a qualified electronic signature has the legal equivalent of a handwritten signature across all EU member states.
questions.shortAnswer: eIDAS 2.0 expands the original eIDAS trust services framework with new service types including electronic attestations of attributes, electronic archiving, and electronic ledgers. Qualified trust services must meet requirements defined in the regulation, be provided by qualified trust service providers (QTSPs) that have been audited and approved by their national supervisory body, and be listed on the EU Trusted Lists. The qualified status provides maximum legal certainty — courts and public authorities across the EU must accept qualified trust services at face value.

questions.question: When does eIDAS 2.0 become mandatory?
questions.answer: The eIDAS 2.0 regulation entered into force in 2024, with member states required to offer at least one European Digital Identity Wallet by 2026. The implementation timeline is staggered: implementing acts defining technical standards and wallet specifications are being developed progressively, with key technical requirements expected to be finalised throughout 2025-2026. Very large online platforms will be required to accept wallet-based identification once the wallet infrastructure is operational. Full compliance across all regulated sectors is expected by 2027.
questions.shortAnswer: eIDAS 2.0 follows a phased implementation. The regulation text was adopted in 2024, but practical obligations depend on implementing acts that define the technical standards for the wallet, trust services, and interoperability. Member states must make wallets available to citizens by 2026. Organisations in regulated sectors (banking, telecoms, healthcare, transport) and very large online platforms face mandatory wallet acceptance once the infrastructure is live. Organisations should begin preparing now by understanding which of their identity verification processes will need to support wallet-based credentials.

questions.question: What are the eIDAS 2.0 European Digital Identity Wallet requirements?
questions.answer: The eIDAS 2.0 regulation requires every EU member state to offer at least one European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDIW) to its citizens by 2026. The wallet must enable citizens to securely store and present digital identity credentials, electronic attestations of attributes (such as diplomas, driving licences, and professional qualifications), and electronic signatures. The wallet must be free for natural persons, interoperable across all member states, ensure user control over data sharing through selective disclosure, and meet stringent security certification requirements.
questions.shortAnswer: The EUDIW is a core component of the revised eIDAS regulation. Every EU citizen will have the right to a digital identity wallet that stores government-issued identity credentials and third-party attestations. The wallet operates on a decentralised model where the user controls which information is shared with relying parties — including the ability to disclose only specific attributes (for example, proving you are over 18 without revealing your exact date of birth). Large online platforms and certain regulated sectors will be required to accept wallet-based identification.

questions.question: Is the EU Digital Identity Wallet mandatory?
questions.answer: The EU Digital Identity Wallet is mandatory in the sense that every Member State must offer at least one wallet to all citizens and residents within 24 months of the Commission adopting the implementing acts, and public sector bodies and very large online platforms must accept it for authentication. However, no citizen is required to use the wallet — adoption by individuals is voluntary, while acceptance by designated service providers is compulsory.
questions.shortAnswer: It depends on which side of the wallet you are on. Member States are mandated to provide EU Digital Identity Wallets. Public services and very large online platforms are mandated to accept them. But individual citizens and residents are never compelled to use one — wallet adoption is voluntary for natural persons. The mandatory obligations fall on governments (to issue), public services (to accept), and designated private platforms (to accept), not on individuals.

questions.question: Does the EU AI Act apply alongside the MDR for medical devices?
questions.answer: Yes. AI-powered medical devices must comply with both the MDR and the EU AI Act simultaneously. The AI Act classifies medical devices that are already subject to Notified Body conformity assessment under MDR as high-risk AI systems by default (through Annex I, Section A). However, the AI Act aims to minimise duplication by integrating AI-specific requirements into the existing MDR conformity assessment process — the Notified Body that assesses MDR compliance also assesses AI Act compliance for these devices, using a single conformity assessment procedure.
questions.shortAnswer: The AI Act and MDR operate together for AI medical devices. The AI Act defers to existing sectoral legislation where possible — for medical devices, this means the MDR conformity assessment process is the primary vehicle for demonstrating AI Act compliance. However, the AI Act adds specific requirements that go beyond traditional MDR assessment, including AI-specific risk management, data governance for training data, transparency about AI functioning, and human oversight provisions. Manufacturers must address both frameworks, but through a coordinated process rather than two separate certifications.

questions.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to startups?
questions.answer: Yes, the EU AI Act applies to startups that develop or deploy AI systems in the EU. However, startups benefit from proportionally lower fine caps, priority access to regulatory sandboxes, reduced conformity assessment fees, and simplified documentation requirements for SMEs.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act does not exempt startups from compliance. If your startup develops or deploys AI systems that fall within the Act's scope, you must comply with the applicable obligations — prohibited practices, high-risk requirements, GPAI model rules, or transparency obligations, depending on what your AI does. However, the Act includes several startup-friendly provisions: proportionally lower administrative fines (Article 99(6) — the lower of the two penalty amounts applies), priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes (Article 57), reduced fees for conformity assessment by notified bodies, and tailored guidance from the AI Office. The Commission and member states are also required to consider SME interests when developing implementing acts and standards.

questions.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to UK companies after Brexit?
questions.answer: Yes. The EU AI Act applies to UK companies that place AI systems on the EU market or whose AI system outputs are used within the EU. Post-Brexit, UK companies are treated as third-country providers and must appoint an EU-based authorised representative. The UK's own AI regulatory framework is separate and does not provide equivalence.
questions.shortAnswer: Since Brexit, UK companies are treated as third-country entities under the EU AI Act. Article 2(1) applies the Act to providers placing AI systems on the EU market regardless of where they are established, and to providers and deployers in third countries where the AI system's output is used in the EU. UK companies serving EU customers, selling into EU markets, or producing AI outputs consumed in the EU must comply with the full EU AI Act. Article 22 requires UK providers of high-risk AI systems to appoint an authorised representative established in the EU before making their systems available on the EU market.

questions.question: What does the EU AI Act say about biometric identification?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act heavily restricts biometric AI. Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces is banned for law enforcement with narrow exceptions. Biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes is prohibited outright. All other biometric AI used for identification is classified as high-risk under Annex III Category 1, requiring full Chapter III compliance.
questions.shortAnswer: Biometric identification receives the strictest treatment under the EU AI Act. Three layers of regulation apply. First, certain biometric practices are prohibited outright: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement (Article 5(1)(h), with narrow exceptions), untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases (Article 5(1)(e)), and biometric categorisation to infer sensitive attributes like race, religion, or sexual orientation (Article 5(1)(g)). Second, all other biometric identification and categorisation AI systems fall under Annex III Category 1 as high-risk, requiring the full suite of Chapter III obligations. Third, the remaining biometric transparency obligations under Article 50 require disclosure when biometric systems are used.

questions.question: Is emotion recognition AI banned under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: Emotion recognition AI is banned in workplaces and educational institutions under Article 5(1)(f), with exceptions only for medical or safety purposes. Outside these contexts, emotion recognition is not banned but is subject to transparency obligations — users must be informed they are being subjected to emotion recognition.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act takes a targeted approach to emotion recognition. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits AI systems that infer emotions of natural persons in the areas of workplace and educational institutions, except where the AI system is intended for medical or safety reasons. This means employee sentiment analysis tools, student engagement monitors, and workplace mood detection are banned. Outside workplaces and education, emotion recognition is permitted but requires transparency disclosure under Article 50(3) — the person must be informed that they are being exposed to an emotion recognition system. Emotion recognition in the context of biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes is separately prohibited under Article 5(1)(g).

questions.question: When does the EU AI Act come into force and what are the key deadlines?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It follows a phased implementation schedule under Article 113: prohibited AI practices and AI literacy apply from 2 February 2025, GPAI model obligations and governance provisions from 2 August 2025, and the remainder of the Regulation from 2 August 2026. The high-risk obligations were deferred by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026) and now apply from 2 December 2027 for standalone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in Annex I products.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act (Regulation EU 2024/1689) was published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 12 July 2024 and entered into force on 1 August 2024. Rather than applying all at once, Article 113 establishes a phased timeline, now stretching from February 2025 through August 2028, giving organisations progressively more time for the most complex obligations.

questions.question: How does the EU AI Act affect AI in financial services?
questions.answer: AI used for credit scoring, insurance risk assessment, and insurance pricing is classified as high-risk under Annex III Category 5. Financial institutions using AI for these purposes must comply with full Chapter III requirements alongside existing financial regulation (CRD, Solvency II, MiFID II, DORA). The AI Act adds risk management, documentation, and human oversight obligations on top of financial sector rules.
questions.shortAnswer: Financial services AI is regulated under Annex III Category 5 (access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits). AI systems used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score are explicitly high-risk. AI used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance is high-risk. AI used in financial services also intersects with DORA (ICT risk management), CRD IV/V (credit risk modelling), MiFID II (algorithmic trading), and Solvency II (insurance risk). The AI Act does not replace these frameworks — it adds a layer of AI-specific obligations.

questions.question: What are the EU AI Act requirements for healthcare AI?
questions.answer: Healthcare AI faces dual regulation under the EU AI Act and EU medical device regulations. AI in medical devices is high-risk under Annex I (MDR/IVDR pathway). AI used for healthcare access decisions or triage is high-risk under Annex III. Clinical AI must comply with both frameworks simultaneously, plus sector-specific rules.
questions.shortAnswer: Healthcare AI enters the EU AI Act through multiple pathways. AI systems that are medical devices or in vitro diagnostic devices are high-risk under Article 6(1) via Annex I, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR 2017/745) and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR 2017/746). AI systems used for decisions affecting access to healthcare services, emergency dispatch prioritisation, or health insurance are high-risk under Annex III Category 5. AI used in clinical decision support, diagnostic assistance, or treatment recommendation faces the heaviest compliance burden because it must satisfy both the AI Act and the relevant medical device regulation.

questions.question: How does the EU AI Act regulate AI in HR and recruitment?
questions.answer: AI used in recruitment, candidate screening, interview assessment, job advertising targeting, performance evaluation, promotion decisions, task allocation, and worker monitoring is classified as high-risk under Annex III Category 4. This triggers the full suite of Chapter III obligations including risk management, human oversight, data governance, and conformity assessment.
questions.shortAnswer: Annex III Category 4 (Employment, workers management, and access to self-employment) makes AI in HR one of the most heavily regulated areas under the EU AI Act. Any AI system intended to be used for recruitment or selection — filtering applications, screening candidates, analysing interviews — is high-risk. AI used for work-related decisions — performance evaluation, promotion, termination, task allocation, monitoring — is also high-risk. The only AI in the employment context that might escape high-risk classification is AI performing narrow procedural tasks that do not influence substantive decisions about individuals.

questions.question: How much are the penalties under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act imposes fines up to 35 million euros or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited AI practices, up to 15 million euros or 3% for high-risk system violations, and up to 7.5 million euros or 1% for supplying incorrect information. SMEs and startups face proportionally lower caps.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act establishes a three-tier penalty structure. The highest tier — 35 million euros or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is greater — applies to violations of the prohibited AI practices in Article 5. The middle tier — 15 million euros or 3% of worldwide annual turnover — applies to non-compliance with any requirements for high-risk AI systems under Chapter III, GPAI model obligations, and most other substantive provisions. The lowest tier — 7.5 million euros or 1% of worldwide annual turnover — applies to supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to notified bodies or national authorities. For SMEs and startups, the lower of the two amounts (fixed sum or percentage) applies rather than the higher.

questions.question: What are the penalties for non-compliance with the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act imposes tiered administrative fines under Article 99: up to 35 million EUR or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices violations, up to 15 million EUR or 3% for most other obligations, and up to 7.5 million EUR or 1.5% for supplying incorrect information to authorities. For SMEs and startups, fines are capped at the lower of the fixed amount or percentage, whichever is more proportionate.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act establishes three tiers of administrative fines under Article 99, with the maximum penalties among the highest in EU regulatory law. The fines are structured to ensure proportionality while creating a credible deterrent. Importantly, the Regulation provides specific provisions for SMEs and startups to avoid disproportionate penalties.

questions.question: How do I apply for an EU AI Act regulatory sandbox?
questions.answer: AI regulatory sandboxes are established by member states under Article 57. To apply, contact the national competent authority in the member state where you operate. SMEs and startups receive priority access. Sandboxes provide supervised testing of innovative AI systems with direct regulatory guidance, helping organisations prepare for compliance.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 57 requires each member state to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, operational by 2 August 2027. That deadline was 2 August 2026 in the Act as adopted; the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) moved it back a year when it entered into force on 27 July 2026, so a sandbox you expected to be open this August may not be. Sandboxes provide a controlled environment where companies can develop, test, and validate innovative AI systems under the supervision of the national competent authority. The application process varies by member state, but generally involves submitting a description of the AI system, its intended purpose, the testing plan, expected duration, and the specific regulatory questions the sandbox will address. SMEs and startups receive priority access, and sandbox participation does not exempt organisations from compliance but provides a guided pathway to achieving it.

questions.question: What are the transparency obligations under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act imposes transparency obligations at multiple levels. Article 50 requires disclosure when users interact with AI (chatbots), labelling of AI-generated content (deepfakes, synthetic media), and notification of emotion recognition. Article 13 requires providers of high-risk systems to make systems sufficiently transparent for deployers to understand and oversee them.
questions.shortAnswer: Transparency runs through the entire EU AI Act at three levels. First, Article 50 imposes specific transparency obligations on certain AI systems regardless of risk classification: chatbots must disclose AI interaction, AI-generated synthetic content must be machine-readably labelled, and emotion recognition systems must inform affected persons. Second, Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed in a way that ensures their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. Third, Article 53 requires GPAI model providers to provide transparency through technical documentation and downstream information.

questions.question: EU AI Act vs GDPR — which one applies to my AI system?
questions.answer: Both apply simultaneously. The GDPR governs the personal data your AI system processes, while the EU AI Act governs the AI system itself — its risk classification, safety, transparency, and governance. They are complementary regulations, not alternatives. Nearly every AI system that processes personal data must comply with both.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act and GDPR are complementary, not competing. The GDPR regulates the processing of personal data — how you collect, store, use, share, and delete personal information. The EU AI Act regulates AI systems — how they are designed, developed, deployed, and governed. Since most AI systems process personal data in some form (training data, input data, or output data), both regulations apply simultaneously. Article 2(7) of the AI Act explicitly states that it applies without prejudice to the GDPR, meaning you cannot use AI Act compliance as a substitute for GDPR compliance, and vice versa.

questions.question: What is the EU AI Liability Directive and what does it require?
questions.answer: The EU AI Liability Directive (proposed) aims to make it easier for individuals harmed by AI systems to obtain compensation. It introduces two key mechanisms: a rebuttable presumption of causality (if a claimant shows that an AI provider or user failed to comply with relevant obligations and this failure is reasonably likely to have caused the harm, causation is presumed unless the defendant disproves it) and a right of access to evidence held by AI providers and users. The directive complements the AI Act by addressing civil liability rather than regulatory compliance.
questions.shortAnswer: The AI Liability Directive addresses a fundamental challenge: AI systems are often opaque, making it difficult for injured parties to prove that a specific AI system caused their harm. Traditional tort law requires the claimant to prove causation, which is nearly impossible when the AI's decision-making process is complex or unexplainable. The directive solves this by shifting the burden of proof when the AI provider or user has failed to comply with their obligations (such as AI Act requirements) and the failure is linked to the type of harm suffered. It does not create strict liability — it eases the evidentiary burden within existing fault-based frameworks.

questions.question: What are the EU AML beneficial ownership requirements?
questions.answer: The EU AML Package establishes harmonised beneficial ownership requirements across all member states. All legal entities and legal arrangements must identify and register their beneficial owners — natural persons who ultimately own or control the entity, defined as those holding more than 25% of shares, voting rights, or other ownership interest. Obliged entities must verify beneficial ownership as part of customer due diligence. National beneficial ownership registers must be maintained and accessible to competent authorities, FIUs, obliged entities, and persons with a legitimate interest.
questions.shortAnswer: Beneficial ownership transparency is a cornerstone of the EU AML Package. Every company, foundation, trust, and similar legal arrangement must know and declare its beneficial owners. The 25% ownership threshold triggers beneficial ownership status, but persons exercising control through other means are also captured. National registers must be accurate, up-to-date, and accessible. The AML Regulation's directly applicable rules create uniform standards that replace the previously inconsistent national approaches. Discrepancies between register information and due diligence findings must be reported.

questions.question: How does the EU AML Package affect crypto-asset service providers?
questions.answer: The EU AML Package brings crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) fully within the AML/CFT regulatory framework as obliged entities. CASPs must implement comprehensive customer due diligence, file suspicious transaction reports, maintain records, and comply with all AML requirements on the same basis as traditional financial institutions. The Transfer of Funds Regulation extension (the travel rule) requires CASPs to collect and transmit originator and beneficiary information with crypto-asset transfers, similar to the requirements for traditional wire transfers.
questions.shortAnswer: CASPs are now full obliged entities under EU AML law. This means the same customer identification, verification, ongoing monitoring, and reporting obligations that apply to banks now apply to crypto exchanges, custodial wallet providers, and other CASPs. The travel rule requires CASPs to include originator and beneficiary information with every crypto transfer above EUR 1,000 (and for all transfers between CASPs regardless of amount). Self-hosted wallets trigger enhanced due diligence requirements. These obligations align with FATF recommendations and close a major regulatory gap.

questions.question: What are the customer due diligence requirements under the EU AML Package?
questions.answer: The EU AML Regulation establishes harmonised customer due diligence (CDD) requirements for all obliged entities. Standard CDD includes identifying and verifying the customer's identity, identifying the beneficial owner, understanding the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship, and conducting ongoing monitoring. Enhanced due diligence (EDD) is required for higher-risk situations including politically exposed persons, high-risk third countries, and complex ownership structures. Simplified due diligence (SDD) is permitted for lower-risk situations subject to specific conditions.
questions.shortAnswer: CDD is the foundation of AML compliance. The AML Regulation harmonises CDD requirements across all EU member states, eliminating the national variations that existed under previous directives. Every obliged entity must verify who their customer is, who ultimately benefits from the relationship, what the relationship is for, and whether it continues to make sense over time. The risk-based approach means higher-risk customers receive more scrutiny (EDD) while genuinely lower-risk customers can receive streamlined treatment (SDD), but the baseline requirements apply to all business relationships.

questions.question: What is AMLA and what does the new EU AML authority do?
questions.answer: AMLA (Anti-Money Laundering Authority) is a new EU-level authority established as part of the EU AML Package adopted in 2024. Headquartered in Frankfurt, AMLA will directly supervise the highest-risk financial institutions across the EU, coordinate national Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs), and ensure consistent application of AML/CFT rules across all member states. AMLA will have the power to impose fines on directly supervised entities, conduct investigations, and issue binding technical standards. It is expected to become operational in 2025 and begin direct supervision in 2028.
questions.shortAnswer: AMLA fills a critical gap in EU anti-money laundering enforcement. Previously, AML supervision was entirely national, leading to inconsistent enforcement across member states and regulatory arbitrage. AMLA creates a single EU supervisor for the highest-risk obliged entities, a coordinator of national FIUs for improved financial intelligence sharing, and a standard-setter for harmonised AML rules. It is modelled on the European Banking Authority (EBA) and European Central Bank (ECB) supervisory models but focused exclusively on AML/CFT.

questions.question: What is the difference between the new EU AML Regulation and Directive?
questions.answer: The EU AML Package replaces the previous directive-based approach with a dual instrument structure: a directly applicable Regulation (the single rulebook) and a Directive (the 6th AMLD). The AML Regulation contains most substantive AML/CFT requirements — customer due diligence, beneficial ownership, suspicious transaction reporting, and third-country policy — and applies directly across all member states without national transposition. The Directive covers areas that require national implementation, such as the powers and duties of national supervisors, FIU organisation, and access to beneficial ownership registers.
questions.shortAnswer: The shift from directive to regulation is the most important structural change in the AML Package. Under previous AMLDs (1st through 5th), member states transposed requirements into national law with significant variation, creating an uneven playing field. The new AML Regulation creates a single set of directly applicable rules, eliminating national divergences in areas like customer due diligence thresholds, beneficial ownership requirements, and high-risk third-country lists. The accompanying Directive addresses inherently national matters that cannot be fully harmonised.
