questions.question: What does the EU Battery Regulation require?
questions.answer: The EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542) establishes comprehensive requirements for batteries placed on the EU market covering their entire lifecycle. Key requirements include: carbon footprint declarations and maximum thresholds, recycled content minimum requirements, performance and durability standards, labelling and QR code with digital battery passport, due diligence for responsible sourcing of raw materials, collection and recycling targets, and extended producer responsibility. The regulation applies to all battery types — portable, automotive, electric vehicle, industrial, and light means of transport batteries.
questions.shortAnswer: The Battery Regulation is one of the EU's most ambitious product sustainability regulations, requiring cradle-to-grave compliance. Manufacturers must calculate and declare the carbon footprint of batteries, meet minimum recycled content requirements (increasing over time), ensure batteries meet performance and durability standards, provide digital battery passports accessible via QR code, conduct supply chain due diligence for cobalt, lithium, nickel, and natural graphite, and participate in extended producer responsibility schemes. The regulation phases in over several years, with different requirements taking effect between 2024 and 2036.
relevantArticles: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 — EU Battery Regulation
Battery Regulation Articles 7-9 — Carbon footprint requirements
Battery Regulation Article 8 — Recycled content requirements

questions.question: What does the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive require?
questions.answer: The CSDDD requires large EU companies and qualifying non-EU companies to identify, prevent, mitigate, and account for adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their own operations, subsidiaries, and value chains. Companies must integrate due diligence into policies and risk management, identify actual and potential adverse impacts, prevent and mitigate impacts, establish complaints mechanisms, monitor due diligence effectiveness, and publicly communicate. The directive also requires companies to adopt climate transition plans aligned with the Paris Agreement. Penalties include fines up to 5% of worldwide net turnover.
questions.shortAnswer: The CSDDD creates mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence for the largest companies operating in the EU. Unlike voluntary frameworks (UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines), the CSDDD imposes legally binding obligations with significant financial penalties. The scope covers the entire value chain — from raw material extraction through end-use. Companies must actively identify risks, take action to address them, and report on their efforts. Directors have a duty of care to ensure due diligence is implemented. Civil liability provisions allow affected persons to seek compensation.
relevantArticles: CSDDD Article 5 — Integration of due diligence into policies
CSDDD Articles 6-8 — Identification, prevention, and mitigation of adverse impacts
CSDDD Article 9 — Complaints mechanism

questions.question: What are the requirements of the EU Cyber Resilience Act?
questions.answer: The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) establishes cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements — any software or hardware product that connects directly or indirectly to a network. Requirements include: security by design, vulnerability handling processes, security updates for the product's expected lifetime (minimum 5 years), incident and vulnerability reporting to ENISA, technical documentation, and CE marking. The CRA applies to manufacturers, importers, and distributors. Critical products (Classes I and II) require third-party conformity assessment. Default products can use self-assessment.
questions.shortAnswer: The CRA fills a major gap in EU product regulation — previously, most software and connected devices had no mandatory cybersecurity requirements. The Act requires manufacturers to design products with security in mind, handle vulnerabilities throughout the product lifecycle, provide security updates, and report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA within 24 hours. Products must carry CE marking demonstrating compliance. The CRA applies broadly — from consumer IoT devices to enterprise software — with stricter requirements for critical products like operating systems, firewalls, and industrial control systems.
relevantArticles: CRA Annex I — Essential cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements
CRA Annex II — Vulnerability handling requirements
CRA Annex III — Categories of critical products (Class I and Class II)

questions.question: What content moderation obligations does the DSA impose?
questions.answer: The Digital Services Act (DSA) imposes tiered content moderation obligations based on the type of intermediary service. All intermediary services must designate a point of contact, publish transparency reports, and cooperate with authorities. Hosting services must implement notice-and-action mechanisms for illegal content. Online platforms must provide statement of reasons for content moderation decisions, offer internal complaint mechanisms, and use trusted flaggers. Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs, 45M+ users) must also conduct systemic risk assessments, audit algorithmic systems, and provide content recommendation transparency.
questions.shortAnswer: The DSA creates a graduated system of obligations. Every intermediary service has baseline obligations. Hosting services add notice-and-action requirements. Online platforms add user rights, transparency, and advertising rules. VLOPs and VLOSEs (Very Large Online Search Engines) face the most demanding requirements including systemic risk assessment, independent auditing, and data access for researchers. The DSA does not define what content is illegal — it defers to member state and EU law for that. Instead, it establishes the procedures platforms must follow when dealing with content that is or may be illegal.
relevantArticles: DSA Articles 11-15 — Obligations for all intermediary services
DSA Articles 16-18 — Additional obligations for hosting services
DSA Articles 19-28 — Additional obligations for online platforms
DSA Articles 33-43 — Additional obligations for VLOPs and VLOSEs
DSA Article 34 — Risk assessment obligations for VLOPs

questions.question: What does EU Taxonomy alignment mean for investments?
questions.answer: EU Taxonomy alignment means an economic activity substantially contributes to at least one of six environmental objectives (climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention, and protection of biodiversity and ecosystems), does no significant harm (DNSH) to any of the other five objectives, and complies with minimum social safeguards based on the OECD Guidelines and UN Guiding Principles. Financial products must disclose their percentage of Taxonomy-aligned investments in pre-contractual and periodic reports.
questions.shortAnswer: EU Taxonomy alignment is the gold standard for green investments. An activity is Taxonomy-aligned only if it makes a substantial contribution to an environmental objective, does not significantly harm any other environmental objective, and meets minimum social safeguards. Financial products must disclose what percentage of their investments are Taxonomy-aligned — a key metric for comparing the sustainability credentials of investment products.
relevantArticles: Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 Article 3 — Criteria for environmentally sustainable economic activities
Taxonomy Regulation Article 9 — Six environmental objectives
Climate Delegated Act (EU) 2021/2139 — Technical screening criteria for climate objectives
SFDR Delegated Regulation Article 5-6 — Pre-contractual Taxonomy disclosure requirements

questions.question: What is the difference between 510(k) and De Novo for SaMD?
questions.answer: A 510(k) submission demonstrates that your SaMD is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate device — it requires identifying an existing device with similar intended use and technological characteristics. De Novo classification is for novel SaMD that has no predicate device but presents low to moderate risk. The 510(k) pathway is faster and less expensive when a good predicate exists. De Novo is the appropriate path when your SaMD is genuinely first-of-its-kind and does not fit neatly into an existing device classification.
questions.shortAnswer: The 510(k) pathway assumes your device is similar to something the FDA has already cleared — you demonstrate substantial equivalence in intended use and technology. De Novo assumes your device is new and different but not high-risk — you demonstrate safety and effectiveness for a novel device type without needing a predicate. For AI/ML SaMD, De Novo has become increasingly common because many AI-based tools lack traditional predicates. Once a De Novo is granted, it creates a new classification regulation that future similar devices can reference through the 510(k) pathway.
relevantArticles: Section 510(k) of the FD&C Act — Premarket notification requirements
Section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act — De Novo classification process

questions.question: What is the FDA's AI/ML action plan for medical devices?
questions.answer: The FDA's Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning Action Plan outlines the agency's approach to regulating AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device. Key elements include the Predetermined Change Control Plan framework for iterative algorithm updates, a commitment to developing good machine learning practices (GMLP), guidance on algorithm transparency and bias, support for real-world performance monitoring, and regulatory frameworks that accommodate continuous learning systems. The action plan balances enabling AI/ML innovation in healthcare with ensuring patient safety.
questions.shortAnswer: The FDA's AI/ML action plan is a five-part strategy addressing the unique challenges of regulating software that can change and improve over time. It covers: a tailored regulatory framework for modifications (PCCPs), good machine learning practices as a foundation for safe AI/ML development, a patient-centred approach involving transparency and bias mitigation, real-world performance monitoring through post-market surveillance, and harmonisation with international regulators. The plan recognises that traditional device regulation needs adaptation for AI/ML while maintaining the core safety mission.
relevantArticles: FDA AI/ML-Based SaMD Action Plan (January 2021) — Five-part regulatory strategy
Good Machine Learning Practice Guiding Principles (FDA/HC/MHRA) — 10 principles for safe AI/ML
FDA Guidance: PCCP for AI/ML-Enabled Device Software Functions — Change control framework
FDA Guidance: Clinical Decision Support Software — Regulatory scope for CDS tools

questions.question: What are the FDA classification levels for Software as a Medical Device?
questions.answer: The FDA classifies Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) into Class I, II, or III based on the risk the software poses to patients. Classification depends on the significance of the information provided by the SaMD (treat or diagnose, drive clinical management, inform clinical management) and the seriousness of the health condition (critical, serious, non-serious). Most AI/ML-based diagnostic and clinical decision support software falls into Class II, requiring 510(k) clearance or De Novo classification. Class III requires the most stringent Premarket Approval (PMA) pathway.
questions.shortAnswer: The FDA uses a risk-based framework aligned with the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) SaMD categories. The framework considers two factors: the significance of the information the SaMD provides to healthcare decisions (from informing management to treating/diagnosing) and the seriousness of the health condition (non-serious, serious, or critical). The intersection of these factors determines whether the SaMD is Class I (lowest risk, generally exempt from premarket review), Class II (moderate risk, 510(k) or De Novo), or Class III (highest risk, PMA).
relevantArticles: 21 CFR Part 820 — Quality System Regulation applicable to all SaMD classes
Section 513(a) of the FD&C Act — Device classification criteria
FDA Guidance: Software as a Medical Device (IMDRF) — International SaMD categorisation framework
Section 520(o) of the FD&C Act — Clinical decision support software exemptions

questions.question: Is clinical validation required for FDA SaMD submissions?
questions.answer: Clinical validation is required for most SaMD submissions to demonstrate that the software produces clinically meaningful outputs and achieves its intended clinical purpose. The extent of clinical evidence depends on the risk classification and regulatory pathway. For 510(k) submissions, clinical data may be limited to analytical and clinical performance testing. For De Novo and PMA submissions, more extensive clinical evidence is typically required, potentially including prospective clinical studies. The FDA evaluates the totality of evidence including analytical validation, clinical validation, and real-world performance data.
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, clinical validation is a core component of SaMD regulatory submissions. The FDA expects a three-tier evidence framework: analytical validation (the software correctly processes inputs and produces accurate outputs), clinical validation (the software's outputs are clinically meaningful and achieve the intended clinical purpose), and, for higher-risk devices, demonstration of clinical benefit in the target population. The depth and rigor of clinical evidence scales with the risk level — Class III devices typically require prospective clinical trials, while Class II devices may rely on retrospective studies and analytical performance data.
relevantArticles: FDA Guidance: Clinical Performance Assessment — Framework for SaMD clinical evidence
IMDRF SaMD N41 — Clinical evaluation framework adopted by FDA
FDA Guidance: AI/ML-Based SaMD — Action plan for AI/ML medical devices
FDA Guidance: Predetermined Change Control Plans — Framework for iterative SaMD updates

questions.question: What is a Predetermined Change Control Plan for FDA SaMD?
questions.answer: A Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP) is an FDA framework that allows SaMD manufacturers to describe anticipated modifications to their software — particularly AI/ML algorithm updates — and pre-specify the methodology for validating those changes. Once the FDA approves a PCCP as part of an initial marketing submission, the manufacturer can implement the described changes using the approved validation methodology without submitting a new premarket submission for each update. This enables iterative AI/ML improvement while maintaining regulatory oversight.
questions.shortAnswer: The PCCP addresses a fundamental tension in AI/ML medical devices: regulatory requirements traditionally lock a device's characteristics at the time of clearance, but AI/ML algorithms improve through retraining and updates. A PCCP included in a 510(k), De Novo, or PMA submission describes what modifications are planned, a modification protocol explaining how changes will be developed and validated, and an impact assessment explaining why the described changes maintain device safety and effectiveness. The FDA reviews the PCCP alongside the initial submission.
relevantArticles: FDA Guidance: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a PCCP for AI/ML-Enabled Device Software Functions (2023) — Detailed PCCP framework
FDA Action Plan for AI/ML-Based SaMD — Broader regulatory strategy for AI/ML devices

Section 515C of the FD&C Act — Statutory basis for predetermined change control plans

questions.question: What are the FedRAMP authorization requirements?
questions.answer: FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program) provides a standardised approach to security assessment and authorisation for cloud service offerings (CSOs) used by US federal agencies. Authorisation requires implementing NIST SP 800-53 security controls at the Low, Moderate, or High baseline (depending on data sensitivity), undergoing a Third Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) audit, obtaining either a Joint Authorization Board (JAB) Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) or an Agency Authority to Operate (ATO), and maintaining continuous monitoring. FedRAMP Moderate includes approximately 325 controls.
questions.shortAnswer: FedRAMP authorisation is required for any cloud service used by a US federal agency. The process is rigorous: implement NIST 800-53 controls at the appropriate baseline, document them in a System Security Plan, pass a 3PAO assessment, and obtain a P-ATO from the JAB or an ATO from a sponsoring agency. After authorisation, continuous monitoring requires monthly vulnerability scanning, annual security assessments, and incident reporting. The process typically takes 12-18 months and costs $500,000-$2 million or more. The FedRAMP Marketplace lists all authorised cloud services.
relevantArticles: FedRAMP Authorization Act (codified at 44 USC 3607-3616) — Statutory basis for FedRAMP
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 — Security controls for federal information systems
FedRAMP Security Assessment Framework — Assessment and authorisation process

questions.question: What AI requirements do financial regulations impose?
questions.answer: Financial regulations increasingly impose specific requirements on AI used in financial services. The EU AI Act classifies AI for creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring as high-risk. DORA requires ICT risk management for AI systems. The ECB and EBA have published expectations for AI model risk management. The US OCC, Fed, and FDIC issued interagency guidance on model risk management (SR 11-7). The FCA has published AI discussion papers. The SEC has proposed rules for predictive data analytics in investment advice. Financial AI faces some of the most detailed regulatory scrutiny of any AI application domain.
questions.shortAnswer: Financial AI is regulated through multiple layers: horizontal AI regulation (EU AI Act), sector-specific technology regulation (DORA), prudential supervision (ECB/EBA/PRA guidance), conduct regulation (FCA/SEC/ESMA guidance), and model risk management frameworks (SR 11-7). The result is that financial AI faces more regulatory requirements than almost any other sector. Key obligations include model governance, explainability, bias testing, model validation, human oversight, and ongoing performance monitoring. Regulators are particularly concerned about AI used in credit decisions, fraud detection, algorithmic trading, and customer-facing advice.
relevantArticles: EU AI Act Annex III, Point 5 — High-risk AI in financial services
DORA (Regulation 2022/2554) — ICT risk management for financial entities
Fed SR 11-7 — Model Risk Management supervisory guidance
MiFID II Article 17 — Algorithmic trading requirements
ECB Guide on AI Model Risk Management — Prudential expectations

questions.question: Which countries have GDPR adequacy decisions?
questions.answer: The European Commission has adopted adequacy decisions for the following countries and territories: Andorra, Argentina, Canada (commercial organisations under PIPEDA), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, Isle of Man, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Uruguay, and the United States (under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework). Adequacy decisions allow the free transfer of personal data from the EU to these jurisdictions without requiring additional safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses or Binding Corporate Rules.
questions.shortAnswer: Adequacy decisions are the simplest mechanism for lawful international data transfers under the GDPR. When a country has an adequacy decision, personal data can flow from the EU to that country with the same ease as transfers within the EU. As of 2026, 15 jurisdictions have adequacy decisions. Notable absences include China, India, Brazil, Australia, and most African and Middle Eastern countries. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (adopted July 2023) restored data transfers to the US after the Schrems II invalidation of Privacy Shield, but applies only to participating US organisations.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 45 — Transfers based on adequacy decisions
GDPR Article 46 — Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
European Commission Adequacy Decisions Page — Current list of adequate countries
CJEU Case C-311/18 (Schrems II) — Invalidation of Privacy Shield and transfer assessment requirements

questions.question: Can I use personal data to train AI models under GDPR?
questions.answer: Using personal data for AI model training is permitted under GDPR but requires a valid lawful basis under Article 6, strict adherence to purpose limitation and data minimisation principles, and careful assessment of whether anonymisation or pseudonymisation is sufficient for the training objective. Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)) is the most commonly relied-upon basis, but it demands a documented balancing test weighing the organisation's interests against the rights of data subjects.
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, but with significant constraints. The GDPR does not prohibit using personal data for AI training, but every such use must rest on a lawful basis under Article 6, respect the principles of purpose limitation and data minimisation under Article 5, and implement appropriate technical and organisational safeguards. Where genuine anonymisation is feasible and adequate for the training purpose, it removes the data from GDPR scope entirely, but pseudonymised data remains personal data and is fully subject to the regulation.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 5(1)(b) — Purpose limitation principle
GDPR Article 5(1)(c) — Data minimisation principle
GDPR Article 6(1) — Lawful bases for processing, particularly legitimate interest (f) and consent (a)
GDPR Article 6(4) — Compatibility assessment for further processing
GDPR Article 9 — Special categories of personal data
GDPR Article 17 — Right to erasure
GDPR Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default
GDPR Recital 26 — Definition of anonymous data falling outside GDPR scope
EU AI Act Article 10 — Data and data governance for high-risk AI systems

questions.question: What is the difference between anonymisation and pseudonymisation under the GDPR?
questions.answer: Anonymised data is no longer personal data and falls outside GDPR scope entirely. Pseudonymised data remains personal data and is still subject to the GDPR, but benefits from certain relaxations. The key difference is irreversibility — anonymisation cannot be reversed, while pseudonymisation can be reversed using additional information kept separately.
questions.shortAnswer: Pseudonymisation (Article 4(5)) means processing personal data so that it can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that additional information is kept separately and subject to technical and organisational measures. The data remains personal data under the GDPR because re-identification is possible. Anonymisation means processing data so that it is no longer possible to identify individuals, even with additional information. Truly anonymised data falls outside the GDPR's scope entirely — Recital 26 confirms that the GDPR does not apply to information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person, or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 4(5) — Definition of pseudonymisation
GDPR Recital 26 — Anonymisation outside GDPR scope
GDPR Article 25 — Data protection by design (pseudonymisation)
GDPR Article 32 — Security measures (pseudonymisation)
GDPR Article 89 — Safeguards for research processing

questions.question: Does the GDPR apply to B2B marketing?
questions.answer: Yes. The GDPR applies to B2B marketing whenever personal data is involved — business email addresses containing a person's name (john.smith@company.com) are personal data. However, legitimate interest is often available as a lawful basis for B2B marketing, and the ePrivacy Directive's electronic marketing rules vary by member state for B2B communications.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR applies to any processing of personal data, and B2B marketing regularly involves personal data — named business contacts, professional email addresses, direct phone numbers, and LinkedIn profiles are all personal data when they identify or can identify a natural person. Generic corporate email addresses (info@company.com) are not personal data, but individual addresses (jane.doe@company.com) are. The lawful basis for B2B marketing is typically legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)), which is more flexible than consent but still requires a balancing test and respect for objection rights.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) — Legitimate interest
GDPR Article 21(2) — Right to object to direct marketing
ePrivacy Directive Article 13 — Unsolicited electronic communications
GDPR Recital 47 — Direct marketing as legitimate interest

questions.question: Does the GDPR apply to CCTV and video surveillance?
questions.answer: Yes. CCTV footage of identifiable individuals is personal data under the GDPR. Operating CCTV requires a lawful basis (typically legitimate interest), transparency (signage and privacy notices), DPIA for systematic monitoring of public areas, defined retention periods, and compliance with data subject access requests for footage.
questions.shortAnswer: CCTV footage of identifiable individuals constitutes personal data, and often biometric data if used for identification. The GDPR applies in full. Operating CCTV requires a lawful basis (legitimate interest for most private operators, public interest for public bodies), compliance with transparency requirements (clear signage, detailed privacy notices), a DPIA for systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas on a large scale (Article 35(3)(c)), defined and justified retention periods, appropriate security measures for stored footage, and the ability to respond to data subject access requests for their footage.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) — Legitimate interest as lawful basis
GDPR Article 35(3)(c) — DPIA for systematic monitoring of public areas
GDPR Article 15 — Right of access (including to footage)
EDPB Guidelines 3/2019 — Processing of personal data through video devices

questions.question: Does the GDPR apply to small businesses?
questions.answer: Yes. The GDPR applies to all organisations that process personal data of individuals in the EU, regardless of size. There is no small business exemption. However, some obligations are scaled — the DPO and DPIA requirements may not apply, record-keeping has a limited exemption below 250 employees, and fines are calculated proportionally.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR has no size-based exemption. A sole trader with a mailing list of 50 customers is subject to the same fundamental rules as a multinational corporation — lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, security, and breach notification all apply. However, the practical burden is scaled. The DPO requirement only applies to organisations meeting specific criteria (not based on size). DPIA is only required for high-risk processing. Record-keeping has a partial exemption for organisations under 250 employees. And fines are proportionate — the percentage-of-turnover calculation naturally scales penalties to business size.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 2 — Material scope (no size exemption)
GDPR Article 30(5) — Record-keeping exemption below 250 employees
GDPR Article 37 — DPO appointment triggers
GDPR Article 83 — Proportionate fines

questions.question: Does the GDPR apply to US companies?
questions.answer: Yes, if the US company offers goods or services to individuals in the EU (regardless of payment) or monitors the behaviour of individuals in the EU. Article 3(2) gives the GDPR extraterritorial reach. US companies within scope must comply with all GDPR obligations and designate an EU-based representative.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 3(2) extends the GDPR to controllers and processors not established in the EU when their processing activities relate to offering goods or services to data subjects in the EU (irrespective of whether payment is required) or monitoring the behaviour of data subjects within the EU. This gives the GDPR significant extraterritorial reach. A US company with a website accessible to EU users, an app available in EU app stores, or analytics tracking EU visitors may be within scope. Article 27 requires such companies to designate a representative in the EU.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 3(2) — Territorial scope for non-EU organisations
GDPR Article 27 — Representatives of non-EU controllers or processors
GDPR Recital 23 — Indicators for offering goods or services
GDPR Recital 24 — Monitoring behaviour of EU data subjects

questions.question: What are the GDPR rules on automated decision-making?
questions.answer: Article 22 gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significant effects. Exceptions exist for contract performance, legal authorisation, and explicit consent — but even then, safeguards including human intervention must be available.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 22(1) establishes a default right: the data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them. This covers automated credit decisions, algorithmic hiring decisions, automated insurance pricing, and similar processes where no meaningful human involvement occurs in the decision. Three exceptions exist: the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract, it is authorised by EU or member state law, or it is based on the data subject's explicit consent. Even under exceptions, the data subject has the right to obtain human intervention, express their point of view, and contest the decision.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 22 — Automated individual decision-making
GDPR Article 13(2)(f) — Information about automated decision-making
GDPR Article 15(1)(h) — Right of access to automated decision-making information
GDPR Recitals 71-72 — Profiling and automated decision-making guidance

questions.question: What are the GDPR rules on children's data and age of consent?
questions.answer: Article 8 sets a default age of consent of 16 for information society services (online services) offered directly to children, though member states can lower this to 13. Below the applicable age, parental consent is required. Enhanced protections apply to all children's data, including the prohibition on profiling for marketing.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR provides enhanced protection for children's personal data. Article 8 specifically addresses the processing of children's data in relation to information society services (online platforms, apps, social media). Where consent is the lawful basis, the processing is lawful only if the child is at least 16 years old. Member states may lower this threshold to a minimum of 13. Below the applicable age, consent must be given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility. The controller must make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is given or authorised by the parent.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 8 — Conditions applicable to child's consent
GDPR Recital 38 — Children's specific protection
GDPR Article 6(1)(f) — Legitimate interest considerations for children
GDPR Article 12(1) — Transparent, intelligible information

questions.question: What are the GDPR consent requirements?
questions.answer: GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous (Article 4(11)). It requires a clear affirmative action — pre-ticked boxes and silence do not count. Consent must be as easy to withdraw as to give. For special category data, explicit consent is required. Consent is one of six lawful bases and is not always necessary.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 4(11) defines consent as any freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by which they, by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signify agreement to the processing of personal data relating to them. Article 7 sets additional conditions: the controller must be able to demonstrate consent was given, the consent request must be clearly distinguishable and in clear language, consent must be withdrawable at any time, and the assessment of whether consent is freely given must consider whether contract performance is conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for the contract.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 4(11) — Definition of consent
GDPR Article 7 — Conditions for consent
GDPR Article 8 — Conditions for children's consent
GDPR Article 9(2)(a) — Explicit consent for special category data

questions.question: Do I need consent for cookies under the GDPR?
questions.answer: Consent is required for non-essential cookies under the ePrivacy Directive (implemented nationally), which the GDPR reinforces. Strictly necessary cookies (essential for website function) do not require consent. Analytics, advertising, and tracking cookies require prior informed consent with a genuine opt-in mechanism.
questions.shortAnswer: Cookie consent is primarily governed by Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC, as amended), not the GDPR directly. However, the GDPR's definition of consent (Article 4(11)) and conditions for valid consent (Article 7) apply to determine whether cookie consent is valid. The result: strictly necessary cookies (session management, security, load balancing) do not require consent. All other cookies — analytics, advertising, social media, personalisation, and tracking cookies — require prior, informed, freely given, specific consent through a clear affirmative action before the cookie is set.
relevantArticles: ePrivacy Directive Article 5(3) — Cookie consent requirement
GDPR Article 4(11) — Definition of consent
GDPR Article 7 — Conditions for consent
GDPR Recital 32 — Affirmative action for consent

questions.question: What is the GDPR 72-hour data breach notification rule?
questions.answer: Article 33 requires controllers to notify the competent supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it — unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.
questions.shortAnswer: When a personal data breach occurs that is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must notify the competent supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming "aware" of the breach. The notification must describe the breach, the likely consequences, the measures taken, and the number of affected individuals. If notification cannot be made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay. Not all breaches require notification — only those likely to result in risk. All breaches, regardless of risk level, must be documented internally.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 33 — Notification to supervisory authority
GDPR Article 34 — Communication to data subjects
GDPR Article 33(5) — Documentation of all breaches
GDPR Article 83(4)(a) — Fines for notification failures

questions.question: What are the GDPR rules on employee monitoring?
questions.answer: The GDPR does not prohibit employee monitoring but requires it to have a lawful basis, be proportionate, transparent, and documented. Employers must inform employees about monitoring, conduct DPIAs for systematic monitoring, and ensure that monitoring does not excessively intrude on employee privacy rights.
questions.shortAnswer: Employee monitoring — email surveillance, internet usage tracking, video surveillance, keystroke logging, location tracking, and productivity monitoring — is permitted under the GDPR but subject to strict conditions. The employer must have a valid lawful basis (typically legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f), with consent rarely being valid due to the power imbalance), the monitoring must be proportionate to the legitimate aim, employees must be informed about what is monitored and why (transparency under Articles 13-14), a DPIA is likely required for systematic monitoring (Article 35), and national employment law may impose additional restrictions.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) — Legitimate interest as lawful basis
GDPR Article 35 — DPIA for high-risk processing
GDPR Articles 13-14 — Transparency and information obligations
GDPR Article 88 — Processing in the context of employment

questions.question: How are GDPR fines calculated?
questions.answer: GDPR fines are up to 20 million euros or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for the most serious violations, or up to 10 million euros or 2% for less serious violations. Supervisory authorities consider the nature and gravity of the infringement, number of data subjects, degree of cooperation, and other factors listed in Article 83(2).
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR establishes two tiers of administrative fines. Tier 1 (Article 83(4)): up to 10 million euros or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This applies to violations of controller and processor obligations, certification body obligations, and monitoring body obligations. Tier 2 (Article 83(5)): up to 20 million euros or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. This applies to violations of data processing principles, lawful basis requirements, consent conditions, data subject rights, international transfer provisions, and orders by supervisory authorities.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 83(4) — Tier 1 fines (up to 10M or 2%)

questions.question: Do I need records of processing activities under the GDPR?
questions.answer: Yes, if your organisation has 250 or more employees. Below 250 employees, you still need records if your processing is not occasional, includes special category or criminal data, or is likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights. In practice, nearly all organisations need to maintain processing records.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 30 requires controllers and processors to maintain records of processing activities. For controllers, the records must include the controller's identity, processing purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, categories of recipients, international transfers, retention periods, and security measures. For processors, records must include the processor's identity, categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller, international transfers, and security measures. The records must be in writing (including electronic form) and made available to supervisory authorities on request.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 30 — Records of processing activities

questions.question: What is the GDPR right to data portability?
questions.answer: Article 20 gives data subjects the right to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, and to transmit that data to another controller. This right applies only when processing is based on consent or contract and is carried out by automated means.
questions.shortAnswer: The right to data portability (Article 20) gives data subjects two related rights: the right to receive their personal data from a controller in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, and the right to have that data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible. This right applies only when processing is based on consent (Article 6(1)(a) or Article 9(2)(a)) or contractual necessity (Article 6(1)(b)), and the processing is carried out by automated means. It does not apply to processing based on legitimate interest, legal obligation, or other lawful bases.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 20 — Right to data portability
GDPR Article 12 — Conditions for exercising rights (timeline, format)

questions.question: What are the exceptions to the GDPR right to erasure?
questions.answer: The right to erasure (right to be forgotten) under Article 17 is not absolute. Organisations can refuse erasure requests when the data is needed for exercising freedom of expression, legal obligation compliance, public health purposes, archiving in the public interest, or establishing, exercising, or defending legal claims.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 17(1) gives data subjects the right to obtain erasure of their personal data without undue delay when the data is no longer necessary for its original purpose, consent is withdrawn and no other legal basis applies, the data subject objects under Article 21 and there are no overriding legitimate grounds, the data has been unlawfully processed, or erasure is required by EU or member state law. However, Article 17(3) lists five exceptions where the right does not apply, even when an erasure ground exists.

questions.question: What is the deadline for responding to a GDPR subject access request?
questions.answer: You must respond to a subject access request (SAR) within one month of receipt. This can be extended by two further months for complex or numerous requests, but you must inform the data subject of the extension and the reasons within the initial one-month period. The response must be provided free of charge.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 12(3) requires that controllers respond to data subject requests — including subject access requests under Article 15 — without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request. The period can be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests, but the controller must inform the data subject of the extension and the reasons within the initial one-month period. The response must be provided free of charge unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, in which case a reasonable fee may be charged or the request may be refused.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 12(3) — Response timeline

questions.question: How can I transfer personal data outside the EU under the GDPR?
questions.answer: International data transfers require a valid transfer mechanism. Options include adequacy decisions (Article 45), Standard Contractual Clauses (Article 46(2)(c)), Binding Corporate Rules (Article 47), and specific derogations (Article 49). Since the Schrems II ruling, supplementary measures may be needed to ensure adequate protection in the destination country.
questions.shortAnswer: Chapter V of the GDPR restricts transfers of personal data to countries outside the EU/EEA unless adequate protection is ensured. The primary mechanisms are: adequacy decisions — the European Commission has determined the destination country provides adequate protection (currently including the UK, Japan, South Korea, and the US under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework); Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) — pre-approved contractual terms between the data exporter and importer; Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) — approved intra-group data protection policies for multinational corporations; and derogations under Article 49 for specific situations like explicit consent or contract necessity.

GDPR Article 49 — Derogations for specific situations

questions.question: How do the GDPR and EU AI Act interact?
questions.answer: The GDPR and EU AI Act are complementary frameworks with overlapping scope: the GDPR governs personal data processing while the AI Act regulates AI system risk. When an AI system processes personal data, both apply simultaneously, requiring organizations to satisfy data protection impact assessments under the GDPR and conformity assessments under the AI Act, with supervisory authorities coordinating enforcement.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR and EU AI Act operate in parallel. The GDPR applies whenever personal data is processed, including by AI systems. The AI Act applies based on the risk level of the AI system itself, regardless of whether personal data is involved. When both apply, organizations must comply with both simultaneously, and neither regulation exempts compliance with the other.

questions.question: GDPR vs EU AI Act: which applies first to AI systems?
questions.answer: Both apply simultaneously — they are not alternatives. The GDPR governs personal data processing by AI systems (consent, data minimisation, rights, DPIAs). The EU AI Act governs the AI system itself (risk classification, conformity assessment, transparency, human oversight). Where an AI system processes personal data, the organisation must comply with both frameworks concurrently. The GDPR takes precedence for data protection matters, while the AI Act adds AI-specific obligations. There is no hierarchy that exempts compliance with either regulation when both apply.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR and EU AI Act are complementary, not competing. The GDPR has applied since 2018 and governs any processing of personal data, including by AI systems. The EU AI Act adds a layer of AI-specific requirements on top. If your AI system processes personal data (which most do), you need to comply with both. The GDPR's principles of lawfulness, data minimisation, and transparency apply to the data the AI uses. The AI Act's requirements for risk management, conformity assessment, and human oversight apply to the AI system as a product or service.

questions.question: What are the obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models?
questions.answer: General-purpose AI models have specific obligations under Articles 51-56 of the EU AI Act, including technical documentation, transparency toward downstream providers, copyright compliance, and publication of a training data summary. GPAI models classified as posing systemic risk face additional obligations including adversarial testing, incident reporting to the AI Office, cybersecurity measures, and energy consumption reporting.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act creates a distinct regulatory category for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models under Articles 51-56. All GPAI model providers must meet baseline transparency and documentation obligations. GPAI models that pose systemic risk -- determined by computational training thresholds or Commission designation -- face significantly heavier requirements, including adversarial red-teaming, incident reporting, and cybersecurity protections. These obligations took effect on 2 August 2025.

questions.question: Does HIPAA apply to AI systems used in healthcare?
questions.answer: Yes. AI systems that process PHI on behalf of covered entities or business associates are fully subject to HIPAA. This includes clinical decision support tools, diagnostic AI, predictive analytics platforms, natural language processing of clinical notes, and any AI system that ingests, processes, or generates PHI. The AI vendor is typically a business associate requiring a BAA, and the AI system must meet all Security Rule technical safeguards for ePHI. Additionally, AI systems used in healthcare may also be subject to the FDA's regulatory framework for Software as a Medical Device.
questions.shortAnswer: AI systems processing PHI are subject to HIPAA. The AI developer or vendor is a business associate and must sign a BAA. The AI system must implement Security Rule safeguards including encryption, access controls, and audit logging. The minimum necessary standard applies to what PHI the AI accesses. Additional regulatory frameworks — FDA SaMD regulations, state AI healthcare laws, and potentially the EU AI Act for systems serving European patients — may also apply.

questions.question: Does HIPAA apply to employers?
questions.answer: HIPAA does not directly regulate employers in their capacity as employers. However, employers that sponsor group health plans are covered entities for the purposes of those plans, and employee health information held by the group health plan is PHI subject to HIPAA protections. Employment records held by the employer — including sick leave records, drug test results, and fitness-for-duty evaluations — are generally not considered PHI under HIPAA, though they may be protected under the ADA, FMLA, or state privacy laws.
questions.shortAnswer: HIPAA applies to employers only in their role as sponsors of group health plans, not in their general employment capacity. Health information in employment records is not PHI under HIPAA, even if it relates to an employee's medical condition. However, the group health plan itself is a covered entity, and PHI flowing through the plan is fully protected. Employers must maintain a firewall between plan administration and employment decisions.

questions.question: Does HIPAA apply to mobile health apps?
questions.answer: HIPAA applies to mobile health apps only if the app is offered by or on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity (healthcare provider, health plan, or clearinghouse) or a business associate, and the app creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI. Consumer health apps downloaded directly by individuals — such as fitness trackers, wellness apps, or symptom checkers — are generally not subject to HIPAA unless they are integrated with a covered entity's systems. However, the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule may apply to non-HIPAA health apps.
questions.shortAnswer: HIPAA applies to mobile apps that handle PHI on behalf of covered entities or business associates. A hospital's patient portal app is HIPAA-covered; a consumer fitness tracker app is generally not. The key question is whether the app creates, receives, maintains, or transmits identifiable health information for or on behalf of a HIPAA-regulated entity. Non-HIPAA health apps may still face obligations under the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule.

questions.question: Does HIPAA apply to telehealth services?
questions.answer: Yes. HIPAA applies fully to telehealth services provided by covered entities and their business associates. Telehealth platforms that transmit, store, or process ePHI must comply with the HIPAA Security Rule, including encryption in transit and at rest, access controls, audit logging, and BAAs with technology vendors. The temporary telehealth enforcement discretion announced during the COVID-19 pandemic has expired, and OCR now enforces standard HIPAA requirements for all telehealth interactions.
questions.shortAnswer: HIPAA applies to all telehealth services delivered by covered entities. Every component of the telehealth technology stack — video platforms, messaging systems, remote monitoring devices, and cloud storage — that handles ePHI must meet Security Rule requirements. The COVID-era enforcement flexibility has ended; OCR expects full compliance with all HIPAA standards for telehealth.

questions.question: What are HIPAA's breach notification requirements?
questions.answer: HIPAA requires covered entities to notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. If the breach affects 500 or more individuals, the covered entity must also notify HHS and prominent media outlets within the same 60-day period. For breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals, HHS notification can be deferred to an annual report. Business associates must notify the covered entity of breaches within 60 days of discovery, and the covered entity then has 60 days from its own discovery to notify individuals.
questions.shortAnswer: You must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. Large breaches (500+ individuals) also require immediate notification to HHS and local media. Business associates must notify the covered entity within 60 days. A risk assessment determines whether an incident rises to the level of a reportable breach, based on a four-factor test examining the nature of the PHI, who accessed it, whether it was actually acquired or viewed, and the extent to which risk has been mitigated.

questions.question: When is a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement required?
questions.answer: A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is required whenever a covered entity engages a person or organisation that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on its behalf. Under 45 CFR 164.502(e) and 164.504(e), the BAA must establish the permitted uses and disclosures of PHI, require appropriate safeguards, mandate breach reporting, and ensure the business associate complies with applicable HIPAA requirements. Operating without a BAA when one is required is itself a HIPAA violation.
questions.shortAnswer: A BAA is required whenever you share PHI with a third party that performs functions or activities involving the use or disclosure of PHI on your behalf. This includes cloud hosting providers, IT service companies, billing services, consultants, attorneys, and any other vendor that accesses, processes, stores, or transmits PHI. Both the covered entity and the business associate face penalties if a BAA is not in place.

questions.question: Is cloud storage HIPAA compliant?
questions.answer: Cloud storage can be HIPAA compliant, but only if the cloud service provider signs a Business Associate Agreement, implements appropriate Security Rule safeguards, and the covered entity properly configures and monitors the cloud environment. Major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) offer HIPAA-eligible services with BAAs, but the covered entity remains responsible for ensuring that its specific configuration — encryption settings, access controls, audit logging, and data classification — meets HIPAA requirements.
questions.shortAnswer: Cloud storage is not inherently HIPAA compliant or non-compliant. Compliance depends on having a BAA with the cloud provider, properly configuring encryption, access controls, and audit logging, and maintaining ongoing monitoring. The major cloud platforms offer HIPAA-eligible services, but compliance is a shared responsibility — the provider secures the infrastructure, and you must secure your data, configurations, and access.

questions.question: What are HIPAA's requirements for de-identified data?
questions.answer: HIPAA provides two methods for de-identifying PHI so it falls outside regulatory scope. The Safe Harbor method (45 CFR 164.514(b)) requires removal of all 18 specified identifiers and confirmation that remaining information cannot identify an individual. The Expert Determination method (45 CFR 164.514(a)) requires a qualified statistical or scientific expert to determine that the risk of identification is very small. Properly de-identified data is not PHI and can be used, disclosed, and shared without HIPAA restrictions.
questions.shortAnswer: De-identified data is not PHI and falls outside HIPAA entirely. You can achieve de-identification through Safe Harbor (remove all 18 identifiers and have no actual knowledge of re-identification risk) or Expert Determination (a qualified expert certifies that re-identification risk is very small). Both methods require documentation. Pseudonymised or partially de-identified data that retains any identifier remains PHI.

questions.question: Does HIPAA require encryption?
questions.answer: HIPAA's Security Rule classifies encryption as an 'addressable' implementation specification rather than a mandatory requirement. Under 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(iv) and 164.312(e)(2)(ii), covered entities must either implement encryption or document why an equivalent alternative safeguard is reasonable and appropriate. In practice, encryption is virtually mandatory: OCR's breach notification guidance creates a strong incentive because unencrypted PHI that is breached triggers notification obligations, while properly encrypted PHI that is lost or stolen is not considered a breach.
questions.shortAnswer: Encryption is technically "addressable" rather than "required" under HIPAA, meaning you can implement an equivalent alternative measure if encryption is not reasonable. However, in practice, encryption is effectively mandatory because unencrypted ePHI that is breached triggers full notification obligations, while encrypted ePHI that is lost or stolen is exempt from breach notification. The cost of not encrypting — both in breach liability and OCR scrutiny — far exceeds the cost of implementation.

questions.question: How much are HIPAA fines?
questions.answer: HIPAA fines are structured in four tiers based on the level of culpability. Tier 1 (did not know): $137-$68,928 per violation. Tier 2 (reasonable cause): $1,379-$68,928 per violation. Tier 3 (wilful neglect, corrected within 30 days): $13,785-$68,928 per violation. Tier 4 (wilful neglect, not corrected): $68,928-$2,067,813 per violation. Annual calendar-year caps apply per tier, with a maximum of $2,067,813 per identical violation provision per year. Criminal penalties can reach $250,000 and 10 years imprisonment.
questions.shortAnswer: HIPAA fines range from $137 per violation for unknowing infractions to over $2 million per violation for wilful neglect that goes uncorrected. The penalties are adjusted annually for inflation. The OCR has imposed single-entity penalties exceeding $16 million. Criminal violations can result in imprisonment of up to 10 years. State attorneys general can also bring civil actions with penalties up to $25,000 per violation category per year.

questions.question: What is HIPAA's minimum necessary standard?
questions.answer: The minimum necessary standard under 45 CFR 164.502(b) requires covered entities and business associates to make reasonable efforts to limit the use, disclosure, and request of PHI to the minimum amount necessary to accomplish the intended purpose. This means access to PHI must be restricted based on role, disclosures to third parties must be limited to only the relevant information, and requests for PHI from other covered entities must specify only what is needed. The standard does not apply to disclosures for treatment, disclosures to the individual, or uses required by law.
questions.shortAnswer: The minimum necessary standard requires you to limit PHI access and disclosure to the least amount needed for the task at hand. Staff should only see PHI relevant to their job function. Disclosures to business associates, insurers, and other parties should include only the specific data elements required. The standard applies to all uses and disclosures except treatment, disclosures to the individual, and legally mandated disclosures.

questions.question: What are patients' rights to access their health records under HIPAA?
questions.answer: Under 45 CFR 164.524, individuals have the right to access and obtain a copy of their PHI held in a designated record set, including medical records, billing records, insurance enrolment records, and other records used to make decisions about the individual. Covered entities must act on access requests within 30 days (extendable by 30 days with notice), provide the information in the format requested if readily producible, and charge only a reasonable cost-based fee. Denial of access is permitted only in narrow circumstances.
questions.shortAnswer: Patients have a broad right to see and receive copies of their health records. You must respond within 30 days, provide records in the requested format if possible, and keep fees reasonable. The right covers all records used to make decisions about the patient, not just clinical notes. You can deny access only in very limited circumstances, such as psychotherapy notes or information compiled for legal proceedings.

questions.question: What are HIPAA's workforce training requirements?
questions.answer: HIPAA requires covered entities and business associates to train all workforce members on policies and procedures related to PHI as necessary and appropriate for their job functions. Under 45 CFR 164.530(b), Privacy Rule training must be provided to each new workforce member within a reasonable period after joining. Under 45 CFR 164.308(a)(5), Security Rule training must include security awareness and reminders. Training must be documented, and covered entities must apply appropriate sanctions against workforce members who violate policies.
questions.shortAnswer: Every workforce member who handles or could encounter PHI must receive HIPAA training appropriate to their role. New hires must be trained within a reasonable period. Training must cover Privacy Rule obligations, Security Rule awareness, and the organisation's specific PHI policies and procedures. Retraining is required when material changes to policies or procedures occur. All training must be documented and retained for six years.

questions.question: What are the key differences between HIPAA and GDPR?
questions.answer: HIPAA is a US sector-specific law that applies only to covered entities and business associates handling protected health information. The GDPR is a comprehensive EU regulation that applies to all organisations processing personal data of EU residents, regardless of sector. HIPAA allows processing of PHI without individual consent for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations. The GDPR requires a lawful basis for all processing. The GDPR provides broader individual rights, while HIPAA's Security Rule specifies more detailed technical safeguard requirements.
questions.shortAnswer: HIPAA covers only the healthcare sector in the US; the GDPR covers all personal data processing in the EU. HIPAA permits PHI use for treatment without consent; the GDPR always requires a lawful basis. The GDPR applies to any organisation processing EU residents' data regardless of location; HIPAA applies only to covered entities and their business associates. Organisations handling health data across both jurisdictions must satisfy both frameworks, as compliance with one does not automatically satisfy the other.

questions.question: How do you detect shadow IT?
questions.answer: The UK NCSC recommends discovering shadow IT by comparing what is actually on your network against an authoritative asset inventory. Four techniques: network scanners that flag devices absent from your asset list; a maintained asset-management system (the baseline you compare against); Cloud Access Security Brokers that surface unsanctioned SaaS in traffic; and Unified Endpoint Management for unregistered devices. ISO 27001:2022 Control 5.9 makes that inventory a baseline expectation for certified organisations — it applies to virtually every Statement of Applicability and is very hard to justify excluding.
questions.shortAnswer: You detect shadow IT by comparing what is *actually* connecting to your network and cloud against an authoritative inventory of what *should* be there. The UK's **National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)** describes four technical methods: network scanners (find devices missing from the asset list), an up-to-date asset-management system (the trusted baseline), **Cloud Access Security Brokers (CASBs)** to spot unapproved SaaS in traffic, and **Unified Endpoint Management (UEM)** to surface unregistered devices. Network access controls (802.1x, WPA2/3 Enterprise) prevent unknown devices connecting in the first place.

questions.question: How long can I keep personal data under the GDPR?
questions.answer: The GDPR does not set specific retention periods. Article 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which it is processed. Organisations must define and justify their own retention periods based on the processing purpose, legal obligations, and legitimate interests.
questions.shortAnswer: The GDPR's storage limitation principle (Article 5(1)(e)) requires that personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed. There is no single retention period that applies to all data. Instead, organisations must determine appropriate retention periods for each category of personal data and each processing purpose, document their rationale, and implement processes to delete or anonymise data when the retention period expires.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) — Storage limitation principle

questions.question: How long can you keep data under GDPR?
questions.answer: UK GDPR sets no fixed maximum retention period. Under the storage-limitation principle in Article 5(1)(e), personal data may be kept only 'for no longer than is necessary' for the purpose it was collected. You must set, document and enforce your own retention periods, then delete or anonymise data when they expire. Longer storage is allowed only for archiving in the public interest, research or statistical purposes.
questions.shortAnswer: There is **no fixed maximum** under the UK GDPR. The **storage-limitation principle in Article 5(1)(e)** requires that personal data be **"kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary"** for the purposes for which it is processed. In practice that means *you* decide and document an appropriate retention period for each category of data, justify it, and delete or anonymise the data once it is no longer needed.

questions.question: How long does ISO 27001 certification take?
questions.answer: ISO 27001 certification typically takes 3 to 12 months from start to certification, depending on organisational size, complexity, and current security maturity. Small organisations with basic security in place can achieve certification in 3-6 months. Large enterprises with complex environments typically need 9-12 months or more.
questions.shortAnswer: The ISO 27001 certification timeline depends on three main factors: the organisation's current security maturity, its size and complexity, and the availability of resources. A small organisation with existing security controls might achieve certification in 3-4 months with dedicated effort. A medium organisation typically needs 6-9 months. A large enterprise with complex IT environments, multiple locations, and extensive scope may need 12-18 months. The certification process involves establishing the ISMS, conducting risk assessment, implementing controls, building documentation, performing internal audit, management review, and then the two-stage external certification audit.

questions.question: How long does a SOC 2 audit take?
questions.answer: A SOC 2 audit typically takes 3-6 months from readiness assessment to final report for Type 1, and 9-18 months for Type 2 (including the 6-12 month observation period). The actual auditor engagement is 4-8 weeks, but the total timeline includes readiness preparation, remediation of gaps, the observation period (Type 2 only), fieldwork, and report issuance. Organisations with mature security programmes can accelerate the process; those building controls from scratch should expect the longer end of the range.
questions.shortAnswer: For Type 1: 3-6 months total. For Type 2: 9-18 months total (including the observation period). The audit itself takes 4-8 weeks, but preparation and remediation add months. The biggest time variable is how mature your existing controls are — organisations starting from scratch need more preparation time than those with established security programmes.

questions.question: How many regulations apply to AI in healthcare?
questions.answer: AI systems used in healthcare face a complex multi-regulatory landscape. In the EU alone, an AI diagnostic tool may be subject to: the EU AI Act (as a high-risk AI system), the MDR (as Software as a Medical Device), GDPR (for patient data processing), NIS2 (if the healthcare provider is an essential entity), and potentially the IVDR for in vitro diagnostic software. In the US, FDA SaMD regulations, HIPAA, state privacy laws, and FTC Act requirements may all apply. A single AI healthcare product can trigger 5-8 regulatory frameworks simultaneously.
questions.shortAnswer: Healthcare AI sits at the intersection of multiple regulatory domains: medical device regulation (MDR/FDA), AI-specific regulation (EU AI Act), data protection (GDPR/HIPAA), cybersecurity (NIS2), and sector-specific rules. The exact count depends on the product's function, the jurisdictions of operation, and the data it processes. An AI diagnostic tool sold in the EU and US could face 8+ distinct regulatory frameworks. This regulatory density is one of the highest for any technology product category.

questions.question: How do I classify my AI system's risk level under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: AI systems are classified into four risk tiers: prohibited (Article 5), high-risk (Article 6 and Annexes I/III), limited risk with transparency obligations (Article 50), and minimal risk. Classification depends on the use case, not the technology. Follow the Article 6 decision tree to determine your system's category.
questions.shortAnswer: To classify your AI system, follow a four-step process. Step 1: Check whether the system falls within any of the eight prohibited practices in Article 5 — if yes, the system cannot be deployed. Step 2: Check whether the system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I EU harmonised legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment — if yes, it is high-risk. Step 3: Check whether the system's intended purpose falls within any of the eight Annex III use-case categories — if yes, apply the Article 6(3) filtering conditions to confirm or exclude high-risk status. Step 4: If not prohibited or high-risk, check whether Article 50 transparency obligations apply (chatbots, deepfake generators, emotion recognition). If none of these apply, the system is minimal risk with no specific obligations beyond AI literacy.

questions.question: How do you complete the NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT)?
questions.answer: Register your organisation on the DSPT online portal (dsptoolkit.nhs.uk) using your ODS code and ICO registration, work through the assertions or contributing outcomes that apply to your organisation type while supplying evidence for each, then publish and submit before the annual deadline, which falls on 30 June (the 2025/26 cycle closed on 30 June 2026 — check dsptoolkit.nhs.uk for the cycle you are in). Larger NHS bodies complete a Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF)-aligned profile; most other organisations complete the assertion-based standards profile.
questions.shortAnswer: The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is an annual online self-assessment maintained by NHS England. You register your organisation on the DSPT portal, work through the requirements that apply to your organisation type, attach supporting evidence for each, then publish and submit your assessment before the deadline, which falls on 30 June each year. The 2025/26 return closed on 30 June 2026. Larger NHS organisations complete a Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF)-aligned profile, while most other organisations complete the assertion-based profile built on the National Data Guardian's data security standards.

questions.question: How to protect against shadow AI?
questions.answer: Protect against shadow AI in three layers: discover unsanctioned AI use, govern it with a policy and an approved-tools list, and train staff. The EU AI Act makes the training layer a legal duty — Article 4, applying from 2 February 2025, requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting the development of AI literacy among staff and anyone using AI on their behalf. That wording was softened from ensuring a sufficient level by the Digital Omnibus on AI on 27 July 2026, but the duty to act remains. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 supplies the management-system framework to run it.
questions.shortAnswer: Protecting against shadow AI takes three layers: **discover** where unsanctioned AI is being used, **govern** it with a written policy plus an approved-tools list and data-handling rules, and **train** staff so they understand the risks. Crucially, the training layer is a legal obligation: under the **EU AI Act Article 4, applying from 2 February 2025**, providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and anyone using AI on their behalf. **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** gives you the management-system scaffolding to operate all three layers.

questions.question: What are the rules for international data transfers involving AI?
questions.answer: International transfers of personal data used in AI systems are governed by GDPR Chapter V, which permits transfers only where an adequate level of protection is ensured. Organizations must rely on adequacy decisions (Article 45), Standard Contractual Clauses with supplementary measures (Article 46), or binding corporate rules (Article 47). The Schrems II judgment requires case-by-case transfer impact assessments, and the EU AI Act adds additional considerations for high-risk AI systems trained or operated across jurisdictions.
questions.shortAnswer: International data transfers involving AI are subject to the same GDPR Chapter V rules as any personal data transfer, but AI-specific characteristics -- such as distributed model training, cloud-based inference, and multi-jurisdictional deployment -- create additional complexity. Organizations must identify a valid transfer mechanism for every cross-border data flow in their AI pipeline, conduct transfer impact assessments in light of the Schrems II judgment, and implement supplementary measures where the legal framework of the recipient country does not provide essentially equivalent protection.

questions.question: Is ChatGPT covered by GDPR?
questions.answer: Yes. Whenever ChatGPT processes personal data, the UK GDPR applies in full — the ICO confirms data-protection law applies to any AI that processes personal data, with no AI exemption. Compliance depends on the tier: ChatGPT Enterprise, Business/Team and the API are not used to train OpenAI's models by default and come with a Data Processing Addendum, whereas consumer Free/Plus chats may be used for training unless you opt out.
questions.shortAnswer: **Yes.** There is no AI exemption from data-protection law. The ICO is explicit that if a system processes personal data, **data-protection compliance is not optional** — and that applies to ChatGPT like any other tool. So the real question is not *whether* GDPR applies but *how to use ChatGPT in a compliant way*, which depends heavily on which version you use.

questions.question: Is ChatGPT high-risk under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: ChatGPT is classified as a general-purpose AI model under the EU AI Act, not automatically high-risk. However, specific deployments of ChatGPT can be high-risk depending on the use case — for example, using it for recruitment screening or credit scoring would trigger high-risk obligations.
questions.shortAnswer: ChatGPT itself is not classified as a high-risk AI system. It is regulated as a general-purpose AI (GPAI) model under Chapter V of the EU AI Act. The provider — OpenAI — has obligations around technical documentation, copyright compliance, and training data transparency. But if your organisation deploys ChatGPT in a high-risk use case listed in Annex III, such as recruitment, education assessment, credit scoring, or law enforcement, then the deployment becomes a high-risk AI system and the full Chapter III obligations apply to you as the deployer.
