questions.question: What SME provisions does the UK Procurement Act 2023 include?
questions.answer: The Procurement Act 2023 includes several provisions to improve SME access to public procurement. Contracting authorities must have regard to the importance of SMEs participating in procurement. Pipeline notices give advance visibility of opportunities. The Competitive Flexible Procedure enables simpler, less burdensome processes. Unnecessary aggregation of requirements into large contracts is discouraged. Payment terms must include 30-day payment throughout the supply chain. Qualification requirements must be proportionate. The Act aims to increase the share of public spending reaching SMEs.
questions.shortAnswer: The Procurement Act addresses SME access at multiple levels: strategic (pipeline notices and forward planning), procedural (simplified processes and proportionate requirements), financial (30-day payment through supply chains), and structural (discouraging unnecessary bundling). While the Act does not set SME spending targets or create set-asides, it creates conditions that should increase SME competitiveness. The transparency provisions also benefit SMEs by making opportunities more visible and evaluation criteria more accessible.

questions.question: When does the UK Procurement Act 2023 come into force?
questions.answer: The Procurement Act 2023 received Royal Assent on 26 October 2023 and came into force on 28 October 2024. From that date, new procurements must follow the Act's provisions. Procurements that were already in progress under the PCR 2015 at the go-live date continue under the old rules until those specific procurements are completed. The transition is therefore gradual — both regimes will operate in parallel for a period as legacy procurements complete. Full operation under the new regime is expected by late 2025 as in-flight PCR procurements conclude.
questions.shortAnswer: The Act is live. New procurements launched from 28 October 2024 must comply with the Procurement Act. Procurements started before that date under PCR 2015, Utilities Contracts Regulations 2016, or Concession Contracts Regulations 2016 continue under those regimes. The Cabinet Office published extensive guidance, model documents, and training resources in advance of the go-live date. Contracting authorities should now be operating under the new framework for all new procurements.

questions.question: What are the transparency requirements under the UK Procurement Act 2023?
questions.answer: The Procurement Act 2023 introduces the most comprehensive transparency regime in UK public procurement history. Contracting authorities must publish a series of mandatory notices through a central digital platform covering the entire procurement lifecycle: pipeline notices (planned procurements), tender notices, associated tender documents, contract award notices, contract details, key performance indicators, contract modification notices, payment compliance notices, and contract termination notices. Most above-threshold procurements must follow this full transparency cycle.
questions.shortAnswer: The Procurement Act creates a publish-everything-by-default approach to procurement transparency. Every significant stage of the procurement process generates a mandatory notice. The central digital platform replaces OJEU and Contracts Finder as the single source for UK procurement information. Pipeline notices give suppliers advance visibility of upcoming opportunities. Contract detail and KPI publication enables public scrutiny of contract performance. This transparency is intended to increase competition, improve accountability, and drive better value for public money.

questions.question: How does the Procurement Act 2023 differ from PCR 2015?
questions.answer: The Procurement Act 2023 replaces the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR 2015) with a fundamentally different approach. The PCR 2015 was derived from EU directives and reflected the EU procurement framework. The Procurement Act is designed from UK-specific policy objectives. Major differences include: fewer procurement procedures (3 vs 7), a unified regime covering most procurement types, a central transparency platform replacing OJEU publication, new debarment provisions, broader evaluation criteria under MAT vs MEAT, and stronger contract management obligations.
questions.shortAnswer: The PCR 2015 was a UK implementation of EU Directive 2014/24/EU. The Procurement Act is a clean-sheet UK design. The most visible difference is procedure simplification: the Act's Competitive Flexible Procedure replaces most of the PCR's specialised procedures with a single adaptable mechanism. The transparency regime shifts from OJEU-based publication to a UK central digital platform. Evaluation shifts from MEAT to MAT, explicitly incorporating social value. Exclusion grounds are restructured and a debarment register is introduced. The utilities, concessions, and defence/security procurement rules are largely unified under one Act.

questions.question: What are the principles of the Procurement Act 2023?
questions.answer: The Procurement Act 2023, in force since 24 February 2025, sets out four procurement objectives in section 12 that contracting authorities must have regard to: delivering value for money, maximising public benefit, sharing information (transparency), and acting with integrity. It also requires equal treatment of suppliers and consideration of barriers facing small and medium-sized enterprises.
questions.shortAnswer: The Procurement Act 2023 is built on four objectives set out in **section 12**, which every contracting authority must have regard to when running a covered procurement: **delivering value for money**, **maximising public benefit**, **sharing information** so suppliers and the public can understand procurement decisions (transparency), and **acting, and being seen to act, with integrity**. The Act has applied in England, Wales and Northern Ireland since **24 February 2025**.

questions.question: What compliance is needed for a fintech startup in the EU?
questions.answer: An EU fintech startup faces a substantial regulatory landscape. Core requirements typically include: GDPR for personal data processing, PSD2/PSD3 for payment services, EU AML Regulation for anti-money laundering, MiCA if handling crypto-assets, DORA for digital operational resilience, NIS2 if classified as an important entity, the EU AI Act if using AI in financial decisions, and potentially MiFID II, EMD2, or sector-specific financial regulations depending on the specific services offered. The exact requirements depend on the fintech's business model, licensing status, and target market.
questions.shortAnswer: The regulatory burden for EU fintechs is significant and depends on the business model. A payment services provider needs PSD2 authorisation, GDPR compliance, AML framework compliance, and DORA digital resilience. A crypto-asset platform needs MiCA authorisation plus all of the above. An AI-driven lending platform adds EU AI Act high-risk obligations. A neobank needs full banking licence compliance. Start by mapping your specific activities to regulatory triggers, then build compliance by priority and timeline.

questions.question: What documents do I need for EU AI Act compliance?
questions.answer: High-risk AI system providers need technical documentation (Annex IV), a risk management system (Article 9), data governance records (Article 10), a quality management system (Article 17), an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), and instructions for use (Article 13). Deployers need fundamental rights impact assessments (Article 27) and operational monitoring records.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act requires extensive documentation for high-risk AI systems. The core documents are: technical documentation (Annex IV) describing the system's design, development, and testing; risk management system records (Article 9); data governance documentation (Article 10); automatic logging records (Article 12); instructions for use for deployers (Article 13); quality management system documentation (Article 17); conformity assessment records (Article 43); the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47); and EU database registration data (Article 49). Deployers must maintain fundamental rights impact assessments (Article 27), operational monitoring records, and input data logs retained for at least six months.

questions.question: What is a Caldicott Guardian and what do they do?
questions.answer: A Caldicott Guardian is a senior person in an NHS or care organisation responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient and service-user information and enabling appropriate, lawful information sharing. Guided by the eight Caldicott Principles, they act as the organisation's conscience on the use of confidential data. Most health and adult social care bodies in England are expected to have one.
questions.shortAnswer: A Caldicott Guardian is a senior member of staff in an NHS or social-care organisation who safeguards the confidentiality of patient and service-user information while making sure it can still be shared appropriately and lawfully when needed. The role is guided by the eight Caldicott Principles, and most health and adult social care bodies in England are now expected to have one.

questions.question: What is the AI literacy requirement in the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems. This obligation has applied since 2 February 2025 and covers all AI systems, not just high-risk ones. The Digital Omnibus on AI weakened the wording on 27 July 2026: the original text required providers and deployers to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 4 introduces a universal AI literacy obligation that applies to all providers and deployers of AI systems, regardless of risk classification. It requires organisations to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. The measures must take into account the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of the relevant persons, as well as the context in which the AI systems are to be used and the persons or groups of persons on which the AI systems are to be used. The article also states that it "does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual".

questions.question: What is an example of shadow AI?
questions.answer: The clearest example is an employee pasting confidential data into an unsanctioned AI chatbot. In 2023 Samsung engineers entered proprietary semiconductor source code and internal meeting notes into ChatGPT to debug and summarise their work, in at least three separate incidents, prompting Samsung to ban public generative-AI tools at work. Other examples — AI features switched on inside approved SaaS, browser AI extensions, and personal local models — share the defining trait: they run outside IT's review, which is exactly what makes duties like EU AI Act Article 4 AI literacy hard to evidence.
questions.shortAnswer: Shadow AI is any artificial-intelligence tool used for work without IT or security approval. The textbook example is an employee pasting sensitive company data into a public chatbot: in **2023, Samsung engineers entered proprietary source code and internal meeting notes into ChatGPT** while debugging, in at least three separate incidents, after which Samsung restricted staff use of public generative-AI tools. Other common examples are AI features turned on inside approved SaaS, AI browser extensions, and personal local models, all unreviewed.

questions.question: What is an EU AI Act conformity assessment and do I need one?
questions.answer: A conformity assessment under the EU AI Act is the process by which a provider of a high-risk AI system demonstrates that the system meets all applicable requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 of the Regulation before placing it on the market or putting it into service. Whether you need one depends on whether your AI system is classified as high-risk under Article 6 — either because it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation, or because it falls within a use case listed in Annex III.
questions.shortAnswer: A conformity assessment is the mandatory compliance gateway for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act. It is the structured process through which you demonstrate — and an authority or notified body verifies — that your AI system satisfies all requirements for data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, and risk management before it can be lawfully placed on the EU market. You need one if your system is classified as high-risk under Article 6.

questions.question: What is a personal data breach under the GDPR?
questions.answer: A personal data breach is a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data. It covers confidentiality breaches (unauthorised access), integrity breaches (unauthorised alteration), and availability breaches (accidental loss or destruction).
questions.shortAnswer: Article 4(12) defines a personal data breach as a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed. This is broader than many organisations realise — it covers not just cyberattacks and hacking, but also accidental email to the wrong recipient, lost laptops or USB drives, ransomware that makes data unavailable, employee accessing records without authorisation, and accidental deletion of data without backup. When a breach occurs, you have 72 hours to notify the supervisory authority under Article 33.

questions.question: What is double materiality in CSRD vs single materiality?
questions.answer: Double materiality is the defining concept of the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). It requires companies to report on sustainability matters from two perspectives simultaneously: financial materiality (how sustainability issues affect the company's financial performance and value — the outside-in view) and impact materiality (how the company's activities affect people and the environment — the inside-out view). Single materiality, used by frameworks like the ISSB/IFRS S1-S2 and the US SEC climate rules, considers only financial materiality — how sustainability factors affect enterprise value.
questions.shortAnswer: Single materiality asks: Does this sustainability issue affect our bottom line? Double materiality adds: Do our activities affect people and the planet? The CSRD requires both perspectives, meaning a company must report on a sustainability topic if it is material from either perspective. A chemical manufacturer must report on pollution even if the financial risk is fully insured (impact materiality), and must report on water scarcity even if it does not directly cause it, if water scarcity threatens production (financial materiality). The double materiality approach captures a wider range of sustainability information.

questions.question: What is double materiality under the CSRD?
questions.answer: Double materiality is the core assessment principle of the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). It requires companies to report on sustainability matters from two perspectives simultaneously: impact materiality (how the company's activities affect people and the environment) and financial materiality (how sustainability matters affect the company's financial performance, position, and cash flows). A sustainability topic is material if it is significant from either perspective — companies must report on it even if only one dimension is material.
questions.shortAnswer: Double materiality means looking at sustainability from two directions. Outward: how does your company impact the world (climate, workers, communities)? Inward: how do sustainability issues impact your company's finances (climate risk, regulatory costs, supply chain disruption)? If a topic is material from either direction, you must report on it. This is fundamentally different from the single-materiality approach used in US financial reporting, which only considers financial impact.

questions.question: What is a DPIA and when do I need one under the GDPR?
questions.answer: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is a structured risk assessment required under Article 35 before processing that is likely to result in high risk to individuals' rights. DPIAs are mandatory for systematic monitoring, large-scale processing of special category data, automated decision-making with legal effects, and new technologies.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 35 requires a DPIA when processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, particularly when using new technologies. The assessment must be carried out before the processing begins. Article 35(3) identifies three situations where a DPIA is always required: systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significant effects; processing on a large scale of special categories of data or data relating to criminal convictions; and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.

questions.question: What is a gatekeeper under the Digital Markets Act?
questions.answer: A gatekeeper under the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) is a company that provides a core platform service — such as an online search engine, app store, social networking service, or operating system — and meets three cumulative criteria: significant impact on the EU internal market (presumed at EUR 75 billion market capitalisation or EUR 7.5 billion annual turnover), control of an important gateway for business users to reach end users (presumed at 45 million monthly active EU end users and 10,000 annual active EU business users), and an entrenched, durable position (meeting the user thresholds for at least three years). The European Commission designates gatekeepers after assessment.
questions.shortAnswer: A gatekeeper is a large digital platform that serves as a critical intermediary between business users and consumers. The Commission has designated companies including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, and Microsoft as gatekeepers. Gatekeepers face strict obligations including prohibitions on self-preferencing, requirements for interoperability, and restrictions on data combination. Being designated triggers a six-month compliance deadline.

questions.question: What is a general-purpose AI model under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: A general-purpose AI model (GPAI) is an AI model that displays significant generality, is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks, and can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications. Examples include GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama, and Mistral. GPAI providers have specific obligations under Chapter V.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act defines general-purpose AI models in Article 3(63) as AI models that display significant generality and are capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of the way the model is placed on the market, and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications. The definition captures large language models, multimodal foundation models, and other general-capability models. Chapter V establishes specific obligations for GPAI model providers, with additional requirements for models posing systemic risk.

questions.question: What is GPG 45?
questions.answer: GPG45 (Good Practice Guide 45) is UK government guidance, published by the Cabinet Office and Government Digital Service, on how to prove and verify someone's identity. It defines four levels of identity confidence — low, medium, high and very high — built from five checks. GPG45 underpins identity-proofing under the UK digital identity and attributes trust framework. The current version is 5.5 (updated November 2024).
questions.shortAnswer: **GPG45 (Good Practice Guide 45)** is UK government guidance on **how to prove and verify someone's identity**. Published jointly by the **Cabinet Office** and the **Government Digital Service**, it sets out a method for deciding how strongly an identity has been checked, expressed as one of four **levels of confidence: low, medium, high and very high**. The current edition is **version 5.5** (last updated 14 November 2024).

questions.question: What is a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: A high-risk AI system is one that falls into specific use-case categories listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, or is a safety component of a product already covered by EU harmonised legislation listed in Annex I. High-risk systems face the strictest compliance obligations including conformity assessment, risk management, and human oversight.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act defines high-risk AI systems through two pathways in Article 6. The first pathway covers AI systems that are safety components of products covered by EU harmonised legislation listed in Annex I (such as machinery, medical devices, toys, lifts, and vehicles) and that require third-party conformity assessment. The second pathway covers standalone AI systems used in specific sensitive domains listed in Annex III, including biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and democratic processes.

questions.question: What is ISO 42001?
questions.answer: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the world's first international standard for an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). Published in December 2023, it provides a framework for organisations developing, providing, or using AI systems to manage AI-related risks and opportunities responsibly. The standard follows the Annex SL management system structure (shared with ISO 27001, ISO 9001, and others) and includes AI-specific requirements for risk assessment, impact assessment, data governance, and responsible AI development across the entire AI lifecycle.
questions.shortAnswer: ISO 42001 is the international standard for managing AI responsibly. It gives organisations a structured management system for identifying and controlling AI risks, ensuring AI is developed and used ethically, and demonstrating responsible AI practices to stakeholders. It is certifiable, meaning organisations can obtain independent certification from accredited bodies, similar to ISO 27001 for information security.

questions.question: What is legitimate interest under the GDPR?
questions.answer: Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)) is one of six lawful bases for processing personal data. It allows processing when it is necessary for your legitimate interests or those of a third party, provided those interests are not overridden by the data subject's fundamental rights and freedoms. It requires a three-part balancing test.
questions.shortAnswer: Legitimate interest is the most flexible lawful basis under the GDPR but also the most complex to apply. Article 6(1)(f) permits processing when it is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject, in particular where the data subject is a child. To rely on legitimate interest, you must conduct a three-part Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA): identify a legitimate interest, demonstrate that processing is necessary for that interest, and balance that interest against the data subject's rights.

questions.question: What is Protected Health Information (PHI) under HIPAA?
questions.answer: Protected Health Information (PHI) is individually identifiable health information created, received, maintained, or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate. PHI includes 18 specific identifiers defined in the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR 164.514) — such as names, dates, geographic data, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, and biometric identifiers — when linked to health information. PHI exists in any form: paper, electronic (ePHI), or oral.
questions.shortAnswer: PHI is any health-related information that can identify a specific individual. It covers medical records, billing information, health insurance data, lab results, and any other health data linked to one of 18 specified identifiers. When stored or transmitted electronically, it is called electronic PHI (ePHI) and triggers the Security Rule's additional technical safeguard requirements.

questions.question: What is a substantial modification under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: A substantial modification is any change to an AI system after it has been placed on the market or put into service that affects its compliance with Chapter III requirements or changes its intended purpose. Substantial modifications trigger new conformity assessment obligations and may change who qualifies as the provider.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 3(23) defines substantial modification as a change to an AI system after it has been placed on the market or put into service that is not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment by the provider, and as a result of which the compliance of the AI system with Chapter III requirements is affected or the intended purpose for which the AI system has been assessed is modified. When a substantial modification occurs, the modified system must undergo a new conformity assessment before it can continue on the market. If the modification is made by someone other than the original provider, the modifier may become the new provider under Article 25.

questions.question: What is the problem with shadow AI?
questions.answer: The core problem is loss of control over data and accountability. Because shadow AI is used outside IT review, sensitive data can leave the organisation irreversibly — as in Samsung's 2023 ChatGPT source-code leak — and the organisation cannot evidence which AI tools its people use. That breaks the EU AI Act Article 4 AI-literacy duty (in force since 2 February 2025) and ISO 27001's mandatory asset-inventory control 5.9.
questions.shortAnswer: The problem with shadow AI is that it strips an organisation of control over its data and its accountability. Because the AI is used outside any IT or security review, **confidential data can leave the perimeter irreversibly** — Samsung's engineers leaked proprietary source code into ChatGPT in 2023 — and leadership cannot demonstrate which AI tools staff actually use. That visibility gap directly undermines the **EU AI Act Article 4 AI-literacy duty (in force since 2 February 2025)** and **ISO/IEC 27001 Control 5.9**, which requires a current asset inventory.

questions.question: What is the UK DIATF?
questions.answer: DIATF is the UK Digital Identity and Attributes Trust Framework — a set of government rules, owned by DSIT's Office for Digital Identities and Attributes, defining what a trustworthy digital identity or attribute service must do. Providers can be certified against it by UKAS-accredited bodies. Under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, certification (currently against the live gamma (0.4) framework; a DVS Trust Framework 1.0 has been published as the successor) is required to join the statutory digital verification services register and use the trust mark.
questions.shortAnswer: The **UK Digital Identity and Attributes Trust Framework (DIATF)** is a set of government rules and standards defining what a **trustworthy digital identity or attribute service** must do. It is owned by the **Office for Digital Identities and Attributes (OfDIA)** within the **Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)**. Providers are independently **certified against it by UKAS-accredited conformity assessment bodies**. The current live certification framework is the **gamma (0.4)** version, with a **Digital Verification Services Trust Framework 1.0** published as its successor.

questions.question: What is a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) under the DSA?
questions.answer: A Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) under the EU Digital Services Act is an online platform with at least 45 million monthly active users in the EU, representing approximately 10% of the EU population. VLOPs face the most stringent DSA obligations, including mandatory systemic risk assessments, independent audits, algorithmic transparency, crisis response protocols, and enhanced content moderation requirements. The European Commission designates VLOPs and directly supervises their compliance.
questions.shortAnswer: A VLOP is a platform with 45+ million monthly active EU users. This threshold captures the largest global platforms: Google, Meta, Amazon, TikTok, X, Wikipedia, and others. VLOPs face additional obligations beyond those applicable to smaller platforms, including systemic risk assessments, mandatory independent audits, crisis response mechanisms, and direct Commission supervision. The designation makes them subject to the DSA's most intensive compliance requirements.

questions.question: What are the lawful bases for processing personal data under the GDPR?
questions.answer: The GDPR provides six lawful bases in Article 6(1): consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest/official authority, and legitimate interests. Every processing activity must rely on at least one. The choice of lawful basis affects which data subject rights apply and how the processing must be managed.
questions.shortAnswer: Article 6(1) lists six lawful bases, at least one of which must apply for any processing of personal data. Consent (Article 6(1)(a)): the data subject has given clear consent for specific purposes. Contract (Article 6(1)(b)): processing is necessary for a contract with the data subject or pre-contractual steps at their request. Legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c)): processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation. Vital interests (Article 6(1)(d)): processing is necessary to protect someone's life. Public interest (Article 6(1)(e)): processing is necessary for a task carried out in the public interest or exercise of official authority. Legitimate interests (Article 6(1)(f)): processing is necessary for the controller's or a third party's legitimate interests, unless overridden by the data subject's rights.
relevantArticles: GDPR Article 6(1) — Lawful bases for processing
GDPR Article 7 — Conditions for consent
GDPR Article 9 — Special category data (requires Article 9(2) basis additionally)
GDPR Recital 40 — Lawful basis requirement

questions.question: What powers does a Caldicott Guardian have?
questions.answer: A Caldicott Guardian's authority is advisory and influential rather than a formal legal veto. They act as the 'conscience of the organisation' on confidential health and care information, advising on lawful and ethical use and sharing of patient-identifiable data. They sit at a senior level so they can challenge and shape decisions at board and senior-management level. National Data Guardian guidance, issued under the Health and Social Care (National Data Guardian) Act 2018, says public bodies across the health and adult social care sector in England, and organisations contracting with them to deliver health or adult social care, should appoint one.
questions.shortAnswer: A Caldicott Guardian's power is **advisory and influential, not a formal statutory veto.** The role is to be the **"conscience of the organisation"** for confidential health and care information — advising on the lawful and ethical use and sharing of patient-identifiable data, and championing those standards at board and senior-management level. Their authority comes from seniority and from being a respected, impartial voice, not from a legal power to override clinical or operational decisions on their own.

questions.question: Which regulations require penetration testing?
questions.answer: Several major regulatory frameworks explicitly require or strongly recommend penetration testing. PCI DSS requires annual penetration testing of cardholder data environments. DORA mandates threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) for significant financial entities. NIS2 requires security testing as part of cybersecurity risk management. ISO 27001 Annex A includes vulnerability assessment. SOC 2 trust criteria reference penetration testing. NIST CSF includes testing in the Identify and Protect functions. The UK Cyber Essentials Plus includes vulnerability scanning. CMMC references penetration testing for security assessment.
questions.shortAnswer: Penetration testing is required or expected under numerous frameworks, but the specifics vary. PCI DSS is the most prescriptive — annual external and internal penetration testing with defined scope and retesting of findings. DORA requires threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) based on the TIBER-EU framework every three years for significant entities. NIS2 requires security testing without specifying penetration testing specifically. ISO 27001 and SOC 2 expect vulnerability assessment and testing without mandating specific methodologies. The trend is toward more explicit and frequent penetration testing requirements.
relevantArticles: PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 11.4 — Penetration testing requirements
DORA Article 26 — Threat-led penetration testing
NIS2 Article 21(2)(e) — Security testing requirements
ISO 27001:2022 Annex A 8.8 — Technical vulnerability management
NIST SP 800-115 — Technical Guide to Information Security Testing

questions.question: What replaced the Public Contracts Regulations 2015?
questions.answer: The Public Contracts Regulations 2015 were replaced by the Procurement Act 2023, which came into force on 24 February 2025. The Act also revoked the Utilities Contracts Regulations 2016, Concession Contracts Regulations 2016 and Defence and Security Public Contracts Regulations 2011, consolidating them into one statute. The 2015 rules still govern procurements that began before that date.
questions.shortAnswer: The **Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR 2015)** were replaced by the **Procurement Act 2023**, which came into force on **24 February 2025** in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Act consolidated four separate sets of rules into a single statute. The 2015 Regulations have not vanished entirely: under transitional provisions they continue to govern any procurement that *commenced* before 24 February 2025.

questions.question: When does the Cyber Resilience Act take effect?
questions.answer: The CRA was published in November 2024 and enters into force 20 days after publication. The phased implementation means vulnerability reporting obligations apply from September 2026 (21 months), and the full set of obligations — including conformity assessment and CE marking — apply from September 2027 (36 months).
questions.shortAnswer: The CRA (Regulation 2024/2847) was published in the Official Journal in November 2024. It uses a phased implementation timeline. 20 days after publication: entry into force. 21 months (approximately September 2026): vulnerability reporting obligations apply — manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA. 36 months (approximately September 2027): full obligations apply — essential cybersecurity requirements, conformity assessment, CE marking, SBOM, and all other manufacturer obligations become enforceable. Some elements, such as the notification of conformity assessment bodies, apply at 18 months.
relevantArticles: CRA Article 71 — Entry into force and application
CRA Article 14 — Reporting obligations (applicable from 21 months)
CRA Article 10 — Manufacturer obligations (applicable from 36 months)

questions.question: When does DORA take effect?
questions.answer: DORA (Regulation 2022/2554) entered into force on 16 January 2023 and has been applicable since 17 January 2025. Financial entities should already be compliant. Unlike NIS2 (a Directive requiring transposition), DORA is a Regulation — it applies directly in all EU member states without national transposition.
questions.shortAnswer: DORA was published in the Official Journal on 27 December 2022, entered into force on 16 January 2023, and became applicable on 17 January 2025. As an EU Regulation, it applies directly in all member states — no national transposition is needed. The two-year implementation period (January 2023 to January 2025) was intended to allow financial entities, ICT providers, and supervisory authorities to prepare for compliance. Regulatory technical standards (RTS) and implementing technical standards (ITS) developed by the ESAs provide detailed specifications for various DORA requirements.
relevantArticles: DORA Article 64 — Entry into force and application
DORA Article 15 — Regulatory technical standards for ICT risk management
DORA Article 20 — Regulatory technical standards for incident reporting

questions.question: When does the EU AI Act take effect?
questions.answer: The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 with a phased implementation. Prohibited AI practices and the AI literacy duty became enforceable on 2 February 2025. GPAI model obligations apply from 2 August 2025, and the remainder of the Regulation from 2 August 2026. The high-risk requirements were deferred by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026) and now apply from 2 December 2027 for standalone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in Annex I products.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU AI Act was published in the Official Journal on 12 July 2024 and entered into force on 1 August 2024. It uses a staggered implementation with five key dates. 2 February 2025: prohibitions on banned AI practices (Article 5) and the Article 4 AI literacy duty apply. 2 August 2025: GPAI model obligations (Chapter V), AI governance provisions, penalties, and confidentiality rules apply. 2 August 2026: the remainder of the Regulation applies, including the Article 50 transparency obligations. 2 December 2027: the high-risk obligations apply to standalone systems under Annex III. 2 August 2028: high-risk obligations for AI systems embedded in products under Annex I (machinery, medical devices, etc.) apply. The last two dates were originally 2 August 2026 and 2 August 2027 and were deferred by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026). Various codes of practice and implementing acts fill in the gaps throughout.
relevantArticles: EU AI Act Article 113 — Entry into force and dates of application

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — the Digital Omnibus on AI, which re-dated the high-risk tiers

questions.question: When does NIS2 take effect?
questions.answer: NIS2 entered into force on 16 January 2023, with member states required to transpose it into national law by 17 October 2024. From 18 October 2024, the obligations apply to essential and important entities in each member state that has completed transposition. Entities should already be compliant or actively working toward compliance.
questions.shortAnswer: NIS2 Directive 2022/2555 was published in the Official Journal on 27 December 2022 and entered into force on 16 January 2023. Member states had until 17 October 2024 to adopt and publish national measures transposing the Directive, with those measures applying from 18 October 2024. By 17 April 2025, member states must identify essential and important entities. However, transposition progress varies — some member states met the deadline while others are still in the legislative process. Regardless of transposition delays, the Directive's requirements represent the expected standard, and organisations should be preparing or already compliant.

questions.question: What is a DPIA and when is it required?
questions.answer: A DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) is a documented assessment of the privacy risks in a processing activity. Under UK GDPR Article 35, it is mandatory before any processing 'likely to result in a high risk' to individuals. Article 35(3) makes it automatic for large-scale special-category data, systematic public monitoring, and significant automated decisions; the ICO adds 10 further triggers including AI, biometrics and tracking.
questions.shortAnswer: A **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** is a structured, documented process for identifying and minimising the data-protection risks of a project before it goes ahead. Under **Article 35(1) of the UK GDPR**, a DPIA is **mandatory** for any processing that is **"likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons"** — assessed *before* the processing begins. It is not optional paperwork: it is a legal requirement whenever the high-risk test is met.

questions.question: Which regulations require a Data Protection Officer?
questions.answer: Several major regulations require the appointment of a Data Protection Officer or equivalent role. The GDPR requires a DPO for public authorities, organisations conducting large-scale systematic monitoring, and organisations processing special categories of data at scale. Brazil's LGPD requires a DPO (Encarregado) for all controllers. China's PIPL requires a personal information protection officer for processors above defined thresholds. Many sector-specific regulations (such as the German BDSG) impose additional DPO requirements. Some frameworks use different titles but require equivalent functions.
questions.shortAnswer: The DPO requirement varies significantly across jurisdictions. The GDPR's requirement is conditional (only certain organisations must appoint one). The LGPD's is broadly mandatory. China's PIPL and South Korea's PIPA have their own variants. Beyond data protection, some cybersecurity regulations (like NIS2) require a responsible person for cybersecurity, and AML regulations require compliance officers. An organisation operating globally may need to appoint multiple oversight roles across different regulatory frameworks.

questions.question: How do whistleblower protection regulations compare globally?
questions.answer: Whistleblower protection varies significantly across jurisdictions. The EU Whistleblower Protection Directive (2019/1937) requires organisations with 50+ employees to establish internal reporting channels and prohibits retaliation. The US has sector-specific protections including the SEC Whistleblower Program, Dodd-Frank Act, Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and False Claims Act qui tam provisions. The UK's Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who report wrongdoing. France's Sapin II law provides comprehensive whistleblower protection. Many other jurisdictions have limited or no formal whistleblower protection frameworks.
questions.shortAnswer: The EU Whistleblower Directive sets a high standard: mandatory internal reporting channels, protection from retaliation, confidentiality guarantees, and penalties for organisations that retaliate or fail to establish channels. The US offers financial incentives (SEC whistleblower awards) and sector-specific protections but no unified federal whistleblower law. The UK provides employment protection but with less structured reporting requirements. The global trend is toward stronger protection, but significant gaps remain in many jurisdictions, particularly in Asia and parts of Africa.
relevantArticles: EU Directive 2019/1937 — Whistleblower Protection Directive
Dodd-Frank Act Section 21F — SEC Whistleblower Program
UK Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 — UK whistleblower employment protection
Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 806 — Public company employee protection

questions.question: Who is the deployer vs the provider under the EU AI Act?
questions.answer: The provider is the entity that develops or places an AI system on the market under its own name. The deployer is the entity that uses an AI system under its authority, except for personal non-professional use. Providers bear design-time obligations (conformity, documentation, risk management). Deployers bear use-time obligations (oversight, monitoring, impact assessment).
questions.shortAnswer: Article 3 defines the key roles. A provider (Article 3(3)) is a natural or legal person that develops an AI system or GPAI model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) is a natural or legal person that uses an AI system under its authority, except where the system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity. An importer (Article 3(6)) brings a third-country AI system onto the EU market. A distributor (Article 3(7)) makes an AI system available in the supply chain without being provider or importer. Each role carries different obligations.

EU AI Act Article 3(4) — Definition of deployer

EU AI Act Article 27 — Fundamental rights impact assessment (deployers)

questions.question: Who needs a Clinical Safety Officer?
questions.answer: Both health-IT manufacturers (under DCB0129) and the NHS or care organisations deploying that software (under DCB0160) must name a Clinical Safety Officer: a suitably-qualified, currently-registered clinician with clinical-risk-management training who owns and signs the clinical safety case. It is a named person, never a piece of software.
questions.shortAnswer: Two parties each need their own named Clinical Safety Officer (CSO). The **manufacturer or supplier** of a health-IT system needs one under [DCB0129](/regulations/dcb0129/), and the **NHS or social-care organisation deploying and using** that system needs one under [DCB0160](/regulations/dcb0160/). In both cases the CSO is a suitably-qualified, currently-registered clinician with clinical-risk-management training — a person, not a tool, who owns and signs the clinical safety case.

questions.question: Will NIS2 apply in the UK?
questions.answer: No. The EU's NIS2 Directive does not apply in the UK because the UK left the EU. Instead, the UK is introducing its own regime: the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, given its first reading on 12 November 2025, which amends the existing UK NIS Regulations 2018 rather than transposing NIS2. UK firms with EU operations may still fall under NIS2 separately.

Instead, the UK is introducing its own regime: the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, given its first reading on 12 November 2025, which amends the existing UK NIS Regulations 2018 rather than transposing NIS2. UK firms with EU operations may still fall under NIS2 separately.
